title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
claim: At equal training FLOPs, MoR (expert-choice, Nr=2) beats the vanilla Transformer in average few-shot accuracy with about half the parameters, because routing lets it process more tokens in the same budget.
quote: the MoR model, using an expert-choice router and two recursions, achieves a lower validation loss and surpasses the vanilla baseline in average few-shot accuracy (43.1% vs. 42.3%).

title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
claim: At equal training tokens (20B), MoR Nr=2 beats vanilla and fixed-depth recursive with 25% fewer training FLOPs and measured 19% less training time and 25% lower peak memory.
quote: our model reduces training time by 19% and cuts peak memory usage by 25%.

title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
claim: In isoFLOP sweeps MoR beats fixed-depth recursive at every size but underperforms vanilla at 135M; it matches or exceeds vanilla only above 360M.
quote: While it underperforms the vanilla model at the smallest model size (135M)—likely due to a recursive capacity bottleneck—this gap closes rapidly at scale.

title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
claim: Expert-choice routing outperforms token-choice routing at Nr=3; token-choice struggles with load balancing for a long initial phase of training.
quote: using token-choice routing yields lower performance (40.0%) compared to expert-choice routing (42.6%), indicating that routing granularity plays a pivotal role in model performance.

title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
claim: Measured decode throughput with continuous depth-wise batching exceeds vanilla for all MoR variants, up to 2.06x for MoR-4 at max batch size, with slight quality loss; the timing excludes KV cache update cost.
quote: Increasing recursion depth leads to more tokens exiting early and a further reduction in KV cache usage. This, in turn, boosts throughput significantly (e.g., MoR-4 achieves up to a 2.06× speedup with 𝐵 = Max).

title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
claim: With the auxiliary loss, router scores for selected vs unselected tokens are almost perfectly separated, so the top-k capacity cannot be changed after training (no inference-time budget control).
quote: the router outputs for selected and unselected tokens are almost perfectly separated. This makes it challenging to adjust top-k values after training.

title: Adaptive Loops and Memory in Transformers: Think Harder or Know More?
claim: Adaptive looping (Nmax=3) reduces math BPB by 22% vs the base model and beats a 36-layer iso-FLOP model on math BPB by 6.4% with one-third of the layers.
quote: Intriguingly the improvement on math benchmarks remains when we compare against the IsoFLOP model (1.687 vs. 1.801, a 6.4% advantage) despite only having one-third the number of layers.

title: Adaptive Loops and Memory in Transformers: Think Harder or Know More?
claim: More loops add little beyond Nmax=3 (Loop-7 improves 1.7% over Loop-3) and commonsense slightly declines with more loops; the 36-layer iso-FLOP model remains better on commonsense.
quote: When we further increase the number of loops, the performance increase is modest relative to the initial improvement from the base model (Loop-7 improves by 1.7% over Loop-3). Interestingly, commonsense performance shows a slight downward trend with more loops.

title: Adaptive Loops and Memory in Transformers: Think Harder or Know More?
claim: With no ponder penalty, the halting router learns layer-specialized depth: early layers loop minimally, later layers loop more; loop use starts only after validation CE falls to about 3.27.
quote: The onset of the increase in the number of loops occurs at approximately the same validation cross-entropy value across all loop configurations, around 3.27 ± 0.59

title: Adaptive Loops and Memory in Transformers: Think Harder or Know More?
claim: The ponder penalty weight lambda is set to 0, so loop-count patterns are driven only by the LM loss; the paper does not measure compute savings from halting.
quote: We set λ = 0 for the majority of our experiments, meaning the model receives no explicit incentive to minimize loop iterations.

title: Improving Test-Time Scaling with Adaptive Looped Transformers
claim: Post-trained looped models (fixed Ouro, adaptive Ouro, Huginn) have steeper accuracy-compute slopes than the non-looped baseline yet are less accurate over the overlapping compute range.
quote: Yet all three remain less accurate than Standard over the overlapping compute range; the exit gate lowers Ouro's decoding cost but does not close the gap.

title: Improving Test-Time Scaling with Adaptive Looped Transformers
claim: Fixed-depth looping wastes compute: many tokens gain little or get worse from extra iterations.
quote: Fixed-depth looping therefore spends additional iterations on many tokens that gain little or even get worse.

title: Improving Test-Time Scaling with Adaptive Looped Transformers
claim: TaH2 beats Standard at matched decoding FLOPs on AIME and keeps improving with depth ceiling while Ouro/Huginn plateau.
quote: Existing looped models largely plateau as iteration depth increases, while TaH2's gain over the non-looped baseline grows from +2.8 points at M = 2 to +3.9 points at M = 8 (Figure 1b).

title: Improving Test-Time Scaling with Adaptive Looped Transformers
claim: Ouro's exit gate suffers train-inference mismatch because the backbone is trained only at full depth; TaH2 trains on-policy with the decider's own depth decisions.
quote: Its backbone is trained only at full depth, causing a train–inference mismatch under early exit.

title: Improving Test-Time Scaling with Adaptive Looped Transformers
claim: Adaptive depth still costs more than Standard in real serving: 22% more decode FLOPs per token and 30-34% more latency, but better attainable accuracy.
quote: Although TaH2 adds 22% decoding FLOPs per token and 30–34% end-to-end latency relative to Standard (Table 2), it still achieves better test-time scaling and higher attainable accuracy

title: CHASE: Cache-Hole-Adapted Skip Exit for Looped State-Space Language Models
claim: Under strict iso-FLOP (equal effective depth), deeper non-looped models keep a validation-perplexity advantage, though looped models stay competitive downstream with fewer parameters.
quote: looped models remain competitive on downstream benchmarks with substantially fewer distinct parameters, although deeper non-looped models retain an advantage in validation perplexity under strict isoFLOPs comparisons.

title: CHASE: Cache-Hole-Adapted Skip Exit for Looped State-Space Language Models
claim: The stock Ouro gate on Looped Mamba saves no compute (it only relocates readout); actually skipping loops makes perplexity explode, while CHASE stays within +3-4% of full-compute perplexity.
quote: the stock Ouro Stage-2 gate's validation perplexity explodes—by up to +4788% (from 12.2 to nearly 600) and erratically—because a skipped loop leaves the recurrent Mamba state without its update.

title: CHASE: Cache-Hole-Adapted Skip Exit for Looped State-Space Language Models
claim: Naively truncating a fixed-loop model at inference fails because intermediate recurrent states are miscalibrated with the LM head; adaptive per-token exits beat a shared fixed exit depth at comparable executed loops.
quote: Naively truncating a fixed-loop model at inference time is therefore not a viable way to save computation, and no single forced depth is optimal for all tasks.

title: CHASE: Cache-Hole-Adapted Skip Exit for Looped State-Space Language Models
claim: Average exit depth overstates wall-clock speedup (ragged halting); savings appear only when prefill is compute-bound and memory is not reduced.
quote: The average exit depth therefore overstates the achievable speedup—the ragged-halting effect that motivates the fixed-iteration choice of Deng et al. (2026).

title: Fixed-Point Reasoners: Stable and Adaptive Deep Looped Transformers
claim: Convergence of the hidden state to a fixed point can be used directly as the halting signal, needing no learned halting module.
quote: let the model loop until its hidden state converges to a fixed-point, and use the convergence itself as the halting signal. Unlike ACT, the fixed-point halting mechanism requires no external module

title: Fixed-Point Reasoners: Stable and Adaptive Deep Looped Transformers
claim: Learned ACT halting in TRM is unreliable: it halts too early or too late, and on S5 only a few seeds learn to adapt.
quote: In contrast, TRM with its ACT halting mechanism either halts too early, resulting in lower performance, or too late, using excessive compute.

title: Fixed-Point Reasoners: Stable and Adaptive Deep Looped Transformers
claim: On A5/S5 length generalization at length 128, FPRM keeps high accuracy while scaling compute with length; TRM+conv+ACT drops on A5 and uses more compute on S5.
quote: On S5 , it reaches 96.2% ± 3.2%, but uses substantially more compute than FPRM; moreover, only a few seeds learn to adapt, while the others exhaust the full compute budget.

title: Fixed-Point Reasoners: Stable and Adaptive Deep Looped Transformers
claim: Compute-accuracy trade-off of fixed-point halting is controlled by step-size decay rate gamma; larger gamma defers halting and buys accuracy with more compute.
quote: The decay rate thus controls the compute-accuracy trade-off directly: a larger γ spends more compute and yields higher accuracy, while P offers only secondary control that vanishes as compute saturates.

title: Per-Token Fixed-Point Convergence in Depth-Recurrent Transformers
claim: A training-free per-token convergence exit outperforms a router trained to predict convergence from the same model.
quote: a training-free rule that halts each token once its output stabilizes attains uniform depth-8 quality at 4.94 average loops (a 38 percent reduction in average depth)

title: Per-Token Fixed-Point Convergence in Depth-Recurrent Transformers
claim: The learned linear router needs essentially full depth and gives no saving.
quote: The trained router A2 needs average depth 7.99 to reach the same quality, yielding no saving, and underperforms A1 across the range.

title: Per-Token Fixed-Point Convergence in Depth-Recurrent Transformers
claim: Randomized-depth training gives depth robustness; a fixed-depth-trained model is sharply peaked at its training depth.
quote: A model trained at a constant four loops (S0) is sharply peaked at its training depth: loss 1.97 at r = 4 but 6.01 at r = 1 and 2.50 at r = 16.

title: Per-Token Fixed-Point Convergence in Depth-Recurrent Transformers
claim: Useful depth saturates at the training-mean depth (hypothesis from two internal points plus Huginn consistency).
quote: Across our two scales the pattern is exact: trained at mean 4, saturates at 4; trained at mean 8, saturates at 8.

title: Adaptive Depth in Looped Transformers: Diagnosing Learned Halting Gates and Trajectory Readouts
claim: Fixed-prior depth supervision with simple confidence readouts matches or beats jointly trained learned gates; failure stems from the trajectory induced by joint gate training, not gate expressivity.
scale: Ouro-2.6B (checkpoint evaluation); controlled at small MANO model
quote: Fitting gates on frozen trajectories localizes the failure: it appears to stem mainly from the trajectory induced by joint gate training rather than from limited gate expressivity.

title: Adaptive Depth in Looped Transformers: Diagnosing Learned Halting Gates and Trajectory Readouts
claim: Learned gates require more average depth than fixed-prior readouts to reach target accuracy on MANO.
quote: Across three seeds, the geometric fixed-prior trajectory paired with logit margin achieves a favorable frontier, requiring only 1.4–1.6 average loops to reach 95% − −99% accuracy. Learned gates consistently require greater depth

title: Adaptive Depth in Looped Transformers: Diagnosing Learned Halting Gates and Trajectory Readouts
claim: On Ouro checkpoints, post-hoc readouts are highly competitive with the pretrained ponder gate, which is not uniformly Pareto-optimal.
quote: In five of the twelve model–benchmark pairs, the selected post-hoc readout achieves higher held-out accuracy than the gate, though several of these differences are small and reported on single runs.

title: Adaptive Depth in Looped Transformers: Diagnosing Learned Halting Gates and Trajectory Readouts
claim: Large KL-to-prior regularisation collapses the learned gate onto a near-fixed-depth operating point.
quote: large β pulls the exit distribution toward the prior and collapses the gate onto a near-fixed-depth operating point, visible as the gate curve contracting to a small range of average depths.

title: Universal Transformers Need Memory: Depth-State Trade-offs in Adaptive Recursive Reasoning
claim: Standard ACT halting-bias initializations (0 and Graves' +1) trap training in a shallow-halt equilibrium; inverting to -3 (deep start) removes the failure.
quote: both default zero-bias and Graves' recommended positive bias settle into a shallow halt equilibrium the model cannot escape. Inverting the bias to −3 ("deep start") eliminates the failure mode

title: Universal Transformers Need Memory: Depth-State Trade-offs in Adaptive Recursive Reasoning
claim: Applying the ponder penalty directly collapses halting even with deep start; warmup of lambda recovers 34% compute at matched accuracy.
quote: Direct application of the ponder penalty collapses halting even with deep start. Lambda warmup resolves this: the model establishes deep processing during the warmup phase, then the penalty compresses computation to halt ≈ 11.

title: Universal Transformers Need Memory: Depth-State Trade-offs in Adaptive Recursive Reasoning
claim: ACT gives an order of magnitude lower seed variance than fixed-depth processing at similar mean accuracy.
quote: ACT provides more consistent results than fixed-depth processing (56.9±0.7% vs 53.4±9.3%), and lambda warmup achieves matching accuracy (57.0±1.1%) using 34% fewer ponder steps

title: Universal Transformers Need Memory: Depth-State Trade-offs in Adaptive Recursive Reasoning
claim: Running a lambda-warmup ACT model beyond trained depth improves accuracy, with a sweet spot around 2x training depth and graceful degradation after.
quote: Running the lambda-warmup model for 36 steps (2× training depth) yields 66% EM, up from 52% at step 17—a 14pp gain from inference-time compute alone, with no retraining.

title: AdaPonderLM: Gated Pondering Language Models with Token-Wise Adaptive Depth
claim: Learned token-wise halting reduces inference compute by about 10% at comparable perplexity across 70M-2.8B Pythia backbones.
quote: AdaPonderLM reduces inference compute at about 10% while maintaining comparable language modeling perplexity and competitive downstream accuracy

title: AdaPonderLM: Gated Pondering Language Models with Token-Wise Adaptive Depth
claim: Under iso-FLOPs (matched average active tokens), the learned halting policy beats fixed uniform and geometric pruning distributions, so gains come from choosing which tokens to prune.
quote: Uniform performs worst, and Geometric variants remain consistently below Adaptive, indicating that gains come from token-specific, dynamic depth allocation rather than a static pruning distribution.

title: AdaPonderLM: Gated Pondering Language Models with Token-Wise Adaptive Depth
claim: A single shared halting MLP collapses to degenerate all-halt or no-halt solutions; removing bottom-K selection worsens collapse.
quote: the model frequently collapses to degenerate solutions, where either almost no tokens halt across all iterations, or all tokens halt prematurely at the first step.

title: AdaPonderLM: Gated Pondering Language Models with Token-Wise Adaptive Depth
claim: Without strong enough regularization the gate defaults to full-depth recurrence; stronger regularization monotonically raises loss, so lambda and k are required knobs.
quote: In the absence of strict regularization (i.e., lower 𝜆 or 𝑘), the gating mechanism lacks the incentive to halt early, often resulting in a negligible pruning rate.

title: LoopFormer: Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning via Shortcut Modulation
claim: Looped models trail iso-FLOP non-looped baselines on perplexity; LoopFormer closes much of the gap and beats fixed-depth looped variants.
quote: looped models trail non-looped baselines on perplexity, reflecting the role of parameters in memorization. However, LoopFormer closes much of this gap, surpassing even fixed-depth looped variants.

title: LoopFormer: Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning via Shortcut Modulation
claim: Naive early exiting in looped models produces stagnant late-iteration representations (high cross-step CKA, flat curvature/entropy); LoopFormer keeps evolving.
quote: Early-exit looped baselines show flat trajectories on all three metrics and high CKA, indicating stagnation.

title: LoopFormer: Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning via Shortcut Modulation
claim: At a fixed loop budget, the choice of step schedule changes results substantially; best schedules take coarse steps early and fine steps late.
quote: Despite identical compute, performance varies across schedules (spread ∼1.4 perplexity and ∼1.3 accuracy points).

title: LoopFormer: Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning via Shortcut Modulation
claim: Fixed-loop looped models collapse when evaluated off their training depth, which motivates elastic training.
quote: Once trained, their representations collapse when evaluated at shorter or longer depths, since those settings are off-distribution Bae et al. (2024); Fan et al. (2024).

title: T-LoopFormer: Token-Level Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning with Dynamic Routing
claim: At the 24x nominal-FLOP budget (3-layer block x 8 loops) T-LoopFormer outperforms the 24-layer non-looped base; at 12x and 6x it underperforms the base but narrows the gap vs other looped models.
quote: Moreover, at 24× FLOPs, our model outperforms the non-looped base model with 24× parameter.

title: T-LoopFormer: Token-Level Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning with Dynamic Routing
claim: Token-choice routing plus recursion-wise KV cache yields the lowest per-token decoding latency, below both the non-looped base and LoopFormer (2.24x faster than LoopFormer).
quote: compared with LoopFormer, our model achieves 2.24× decoding speed faster than LoopFormer, which confirms that the dynamic token-choice routing mechanism and the recursion-wise KV cache are effective in improving inference speed.

title: T-LoopFormer: Token-Level Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning with Dynamic Routing
claim: Most tokens use at most 4 of 8 loops; depth distribution is long-tailed.
quote: most tokens require at most 4 loops (average depth is 3.69), and the overall distribution exhibits a long-tail pattern

title: T-LoopFormer: Token-Level Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning with Dynamic Routing
claim: Depth is fixed from the token's initial hidden state and not recomputed during looping; when the required depth exceeds the max loop limit (low budgets) decoding degrades.
quote: because the loop count for each token is not recomputed during the looping stage, the token’s understanding of the context may be constrained, leading to degraded reasoning performance

title: RecurTrace: Adaptive Latent Reasoning with Loop-Time Memory
claim: Oracle-distilled sequence-level halting reaches 56.9% on MathQA at ~2.0 mean loops, beating the best fixed depth (T=2, 54.7%) by 2.2 points at matched compute and all adaptive baselines.
quote: RecurTrace achieves 56.9% accuracy with an average of 2.0 loops, exceeding the best fixed loop depth by 2.2 points at matched compute.

title: RecurTrace: Adaptive Latent Reasoning with Loop-Time Memory
claim: Penalty/prior-based halting (ACT expected-depth penalty, PonderNet geometric prior) attached post hoc to a frozen backbone collapses to one loop for all tested regularization strengths; CALM confidence exit overspends loops.
quote: Sweeping each baseline’s regularization strength over {0.001, 0.01, 0.1} leaves all six settings at a mean depth of 1.0, showing that the collapse is not tied to one hyperparameter choice

title: RecurTrace: Adaptive Latent Reasoning with Loop-Time Memory
claim: The two-loop floor, not the head, prevents collapse; nearly all items stop at the floor and a few deepened items supply the whole gain.
quote: The two-loop floor is what prevents collapse, raising the one-loop baseline from 1199 to 1313 correct; on top of it, the learned head adds 53 more by deepening mostly items that benefit.

title: RecurTrace: Adaptive Latent Reasoning with Loop-Time Memory
claim: Fixed-depth accuracy is non-monotone (overthinking): peaks at 2 loops and degrades at 8 and 16, so no fixed budget fits all inputs.
quote: On MathQA, a 1.7B looped model peaks at two loops with 54.7% accuracy, stays near 53.6% at the eight-loop training clamp, and falls to 47.5% at sixteen.

title: RecurTrace: Adaptive Latent Reasoning with Loop-Time Memory
claim: Without loop memory, plain looping of a pretrained block raises NLL at 1.7B-8B; memory reverses this.
quote: At 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, plain looping instead raises NLL by 0.07, 0.05, and 0.06 nats. Memory reverses every one of these regressions and lowers NLL by 0.03, 0.03, and 0.02 nats.

title: Understanding Dynamic Compute Allocation in Recurrent Transformers
claim: Complexity-aligned compute allocation emerges without difficulty supervision, but does not give algorithmic generalization: accuracy drops sharply at unseen input sizes despite extra compute.
quote: compute allocation aligned with task complexity can emerge without explicit difficulty supervision, but such alignment does not imply algorithmic generalization: models fail to extrapolate to unseen input sizes despite allocating additional computation.

title: Understanding Dynamic Compute Allocation in Recurrent Transformers
claim: Decision timing matters: early allocation relies on static structural cues (hub out-degree) while online halting tracks algorithmic execution state, and online halting often reaches lower average depth.
quote: We further find that early compute decisions rely on static structural cues, whereas online halting more closely tracks algorithmic execution state.

title: Understanding Dynamic Compute Allocation in Recurrent Transformers
claim: Training shows two phases: compute rises to near maximum while learning, then is reduced while preserving accuracy.
quote: In the learning phase, both variants rapidly increase their compute allocation, often approaching the maximum, suggesting that the model initially relies on near-full recurrent computation to reduce the task loss.

title: Understanding Dynamic Compute Allocation in Recurrent Transformers
claim: On natural-language math (GSM-Symbolic), neither variant allocates more depth to harder splits; ANIRA-O cuts mean depth from 8 to about 4.1 with a modest accuracy drop.
scale: depth-recurrent Llama (McLeish et al.), size not stated in text
quote: Neither ANIRA variant allocates more depth on the harder splits.

title: Towards Distributed Neural Architectures
claim: Trained DNAs are competitive with dense baselines in vision and language, and compute efficiency and parameter sharing can be learned from data.
quote: We empirically show that (i) trained DNAs are competitive with the dense baselines in both domains and (ii) compute efficiency/parameter sharing can be learnt from data.

title: Towards Distributed Neural Architectures
claim: Module reuse (weight sharing) emerges without explicit incentive; in language it appears random and the authors suggest discouraging it.
quote: Consequently we conclude that module reuse is most likely random in the language case.

title: Towards Distributed Neural Architectures
claim: A top-2 DNA trained to skip 30% of tokens has slightly higher validation loss than a 30% shallower dense GPT-2, i.e. learned skipping does not beat a static compute reduction at this scale.
quote: GPT-2 (30% shallower) top-2 (30% skip) 2.772 2.784

title: Think-at-Hard: Dynamic Looped Transformers for Improved Reasoning
claim: Latent overthinking: in looped models a second iteration fixes some tokens but flips others from correct to wrong, so uniform extra iterations are wasteful or harmful.
quote: As shown in Figure 8, while the second iteration corrects 8.7% of predictions, it also flips 2.1% of correct ones into errors.

title: Think-at-Hard: Dynamic Looped Transformers for Improved Reasoning
claim: With identical parameter counts and data, TaH beats always-iterate baselines by 3.8-4.4% while skipping iterations on 93% of tokens, and beats single-iteration Qwen3 SFT by 3.0-3.8%.
quote: With identical parameter counts, TaH outperforms always-iterate baselines by 3.8-4.4% while skipping iterations on 93% of tokens, and exceeds single-iteration Qwen3 baselines by 3.0-3.8%.

title: Think-at-Hard: Dynamic Looped Transformers for Improved Reasoning
claim: Average depth 1.07 iterations per token gives FLOPs and memory access within 4-5% of the standard model (a FLOP/memory proxy), but measured batch-1 decode latency is still higher than Standard (301.4 s vs 210.6 s), though 2.48x faster than AlwaysThink.
quote: TaH iterates twice on only 6% of tokens on AIME25, with 1.48× lower memory overhead and 2.48× faster decoding than AlwaysThink, while achieving higher accuracy.

title: Think-at-Hard: Dynamic Looped Transformers for Improved Reasoning
claim: Using an on-policy (dynamically recomputed) oracle during backbone training causes training collapse; a static oracle from a separate SFT model is required to break the policy/backbone circular dependency.
quote: The dynamic approach recalculates the oracle using the evolving backbone in Equation 5, facing the same coupling challenge and causing training collapse.

title: Accelerating Large Language Model Inference via Early-Exiting Algorithms
claim: Per-token early exit can paradoxically reduce throughput in batched inference because of synchronization and missing-KV bottlenecks; parameter sharing mitigates this via continuous depth-wise batching.
quote: they introduce a fundamental conflict: the per-token dynamism intended to save computation often creates system-level bottlenecks that can paradoxically reduce throughput in batched inference.

title: Accelerating Large Language Model Inference via Early-Exiting Algorithms
claim: Standard weighted CE over intermediate loop outputs overemphasizes intermediate representations; an aggressive (small) coefficient on intermediate losses plus self-distillation from the final loop works best.
quote: The aggressive coefficient strategy successfully maintained final loop output performance while enhancing intermediate output performance. Moreover, incorporating knowledge distillation from detached final outputs further enhanced intermediate performance.

title: Accelerating Large Language Model Inference via Early-Exiting Algorithms
claim: Throughput gains of recursive models with early exit (up to 2.66x over vanilla) are hypothetical, computed from oracle exits (earliest loop matching the final prediction) and simulation, not from a deployed confidence-based exit.
quote: As developing practical early-exiting algorithms is beyond the scope of this work, we present hypothetical throughput improvements based on an oracle-exiting approach [191, 9].

title: Inner Thinking Transformer: Leveraging Dynamic Depth Scaling to Foster Adaptive Internal Thinking
claim: At equal parameters and data, ITT x4 improves average accuracy more than the Loop baseline that iterates all tokens (1.7% vs 0.3% at 162M).
quote: the 162M ITT ×4 configuration improves the baseline by 1.7% with 4-step deep thinking in 50% of layers, while Loop improves only by 0.3% after 4 iterations.

title: Inner Thinking Transformer: Leveraging Dynamic Depth Scaling to Foster Adaptive Internal Thinking
claim: Token routing cuts compute relative to looping all tokens: ITT costs 84% of Loop's FLOPs at 3 steps and 70% at 4 steps (theoretical FLOPs).
quote: With 3-step deep thinking, ITT incurs only 84% of Loop’s computational cost, dropping to 70% at 4 steps.

title: Inner Thinking Transformer: Leveraging Dynamic Depth Scaling to Foster Adaptive Internal Thinking
claim: Selection ratios trained at fixed values can be changed at inference: raising them lowers PPL, lowering them to 50% keeps PPL near the training config.
quote: we can flexibly adjust token selections to enhance performance (e.g., 10.21 PPL in the 70%, 70%, 90% setting, 0.31 PPL lower than the training config), or reduce token selections to lower costs with no performance loss

title: Inner Thinking Transformer: Leveraging Dynamic Depth Scaling to Foster Adaptive Internal Thinking
claim: ITT x4 at 162M reaches 96.5% of a 466M Transformer's performance (larger model, same data).
quote: ITT ×4 -162M model significantly surpasses the 230M Transformer and even achieves 96.5% performance of 466M Transformer.

title: DND: Boosting Large Language Models with Dynamic Nested Depth
claim: Adding DND during SFT improves dense 1-2B models by 1.88-2.61 points and Qwen3-30B-A3B by 0.87 average over SFT alone, with negligible extra parameters.
quote: DND boosts the performances of the dense Qwen3-1.7B, Llama3.2-1B, and Gemma3-1B by 1.88%, 2.61%, and 2.50% and the MoE Qwen3-30B-A3B by 0.87%, all with a minimal parameter and computing increase.

title: DND: Boosting Large Language Models with Dynamic Nested Depth
claim: Reviewing 20% of tokens costs about 6% extra FLOPs (analytic estimate), and measured batch-1 throughput on H100 is 91.6-93.1% of the vanilla model.
quote: The measurement results in the table show that, while achieving performance improvements, our model consistently reaches 91.6-93.1% of the speed of the vanilla model under different circumstances.

title: DND: Boosting Large Language Models with Dynamic Nested Depth
claim: Sigmoid threshold routers saturate when the target selection ratio is extreme, losing discrimination near the threshold; an explicit distribution-preservation loss is needed.
quote: This issue is particularly pronounced when the target selection ratio is low (e.g., 20%) or high (e.g., 80%), as the model may push many scores into the sigmoid’s saturation regions.

title: DND: Boosting Large Language Models with Dynamic Nested Depth
claim: SFT with ITT-style top-p token selection at the same compute gives smaller gains, attributed to train/inference mismatch and leakage of the selection rule.
quote: we found that when the SFT is conducted with ITT (Chen et al., 2025) under the same computation cost, the performance improvement is not as pronounced.

title: Dr.LLM: Dynamic Layer Routing in LLMs
claim: Supervised routers improve accuracy while reducing executed layers: mean +2.25 points and 5.0 fewer layers per example on ARC and DART across six models.
quote: On ARC (logic) and DART (math), accuracy improves in all cases, with mean gains of +2.25 percentage points (%p) and 5.0 fewer layers per example across six models.

title: Dr.LLM: Dynamic Layer Routing in LLMs
claim: Measured end-to-end generation time falls 15.3% for 1,000-token sequences, with router cost under 1% of latency.
quote: Dr.LLM achieves a 15.3% wall-time reduction (29.21 s vs. 34.49 s baseline), while the router adds only 0.27 s per query (<1% of total latency).

title: Dr.LLM: Dynamic Layer Routing in LLMs
claim: Supervision is extremely imbalanced toward execute; plain cross-entropy collapses to always-execute and weighted CE still collapses on repeat, so focal loss is needed for any repeat decisions.
quote: Plain cross-entropy minimizes error by predicting the dominant execute class, yielding trivial accuracy on skip/repeat. Weighted CE partly compensates, but still collapses on repeat.

title: Dr.LLM: Dynamic Layer Routing in LLMs
claim: Repeats are rare but concentrated in late layers and harder DART levels; out-of-domain transfer costs only 0.85 points on average.
quote: Repeats are rare overall (1–3% of labels) but occur consistently across all datasets, with higher frequency in more challenging DART levels

title: Investigating Recurrent Transformers with Dynamic Halt
claim: Token-level halting in UT gives no compute saving until every position halts, while risking some positions halting too early and freezing their memory.
quote: the token-level halt can limit the writable memory (each position can also be considered as a memory slot with read-write capacities) by halting certain positions too early but without providing any computational saving in return

title: Investigating Recurrent Transformers with Dynamic Halt
claim: Replacing GUT's global halt with token-level halting, or removing gating or transition information, severely harms near-IID ListOps accuracy; none of the variants fixes OOD generalization.
quote: Replacing a global halt with a token-level halt in GUT (GUT−Global Halt), removing the gating (GUT−Gate), or removing the transition dynamics information (GUT−Transition) - all harm the performance severely in the near-IID setting

title: Investigating Recurrent Transformers with Dynamic Halt
claim: With dynamic halting, GUT training runtime saturates near 5 minutes per epoch as the layer upper bound grows to 30-40, while fixed upper-bound variants grow proportionally; at low bounds a no-halt model can be faster because halting computation adds per-layer cost.
quote: as the upper bound is increased to 30 or 40, the runtime of GUT starts to saturate around 5 minutes, whereas the runtime of other models keeps increasing proportionally with the increasing upperbound.

title: Investigating Recurrent Transformers with Dynamic Halt
claim: The ACT-style late-halting penalty requires difficult tuning; beta was tuned on validation and set to 0.1 (0 for Logical Inference).
quote: Note the weight given to the objective LACT typically requires diﬃcult tuning.

title: Adaptivity and Modularity for Efficient Generalization Over Task Complexity
claim: For generalization to more hops than trained, adding layers to a fixed-depth transformer does not help, parameter sharing in depth helps despite fewer parameters, and ACT without sharing only improves efficiency (fewer layers), not accuracy.
quote: In this particular setting adding an ACT mechanism without parameter sharing does not impact performance at all but it improves efficiency in terms of number of layers.

title: Adaptivity and Modularity for Efficient Generalization Over Task Complexity
claim: UT+FiLM and Hyper-UT allocate average depth more efficiently and more in proportion to example difficulty than plain UT.
quote: We observe, in Figure 3, that UT+FiLM and Hyper-UT are more fair and efficient in terms of allocating compute compared to the UT model (HyperUT being the most efficient).

title: Adaptivity and Modularity for Efficient Generalization Over Task Complexity
claim: On ImageNet1k, Hyper-UT matches ViT accuracy while using over 70% fewer layers on average; the authors note layer count is an imperfect efficiency measure because per-layer FLOPs differ.
quote: Though the sheer number of layers is not an adequate measure of efficiency—given that the flops per layer vary across models—we note that, on average, Hyper-UT requires a lower total compute budget per example.

title: PALBERT: Teaching ALBERT to Ponder
claim: PonderNet's sampled exit causes high variance in exit index and poor accuracy; even when the prior mode is the last layer, sampling exits from one of the first 10 layers in almost half the cases.
quote: Even if λ is low enough so that the mode of distribution is the 12-th layer, in almost half of the cases, the sampling criterion forces the model to exit from one of the first 10 layers.

title: PALBERT: Teaching ALBERT to Ponder
claim: PALBERT has the best macro GLUE score among early-exit methods (above PABEE and sampled PonderNet) and is comparable to full-depth ALBERT, but does not beat plain ALBERT on every task.
quote: Vanilla ALBERT outperformed PABEE on most tasks and is comparable to PALBERT, while the latter has the highest score averaged across all tasks (see Macro column in Tables 2, 3).

title: PALBERT: Teaching ALBERT to Ponder
claim: The Q-exit threshold trades underthinking against overthinking: q = 0.5 is best; larger q often forces all 12 layers and lowers accuracy, smaller q speeds up but underthinks.
quote: We observed that exiting models with q = 0.5 shows the best overall performance for different tasks. Making q greater than 0.5 leads to a reduction in accuracy and can often force models to evaluate all 12 layers of ALBERT-Base.

title: PALBERT: Teaching ALBERT to Ponder
claim: Results depend strongly on the geometric prior over exit layers, which the authors name as the main limitation; at the best RTE prior the model mostly exits at the last layer.
quote: dependency on the explicit prior distribution could be seen as the main limitation of the proposed method, since treating the exit layer index as a latent variable justified its prior distribution.

title: Leveraging Relaxed Equilibrium by Lazy Transition for Sequence Modeling
claim: Tokens differ in how much refinement they need, but UT processes all tokens equally in depth; lazy transition makes per-token refinement unequal.
quote: Our lazy transition is deployed on top of UT to build LT (lazy transformer), where all tokens are processed unequally towards depth.

title: Leveraging Relaxed Equilibrium by Lazy Transition for Sequence Modeling
claim: LT outperforms baselines on machine translation, pre-training, Learning to Execute and LAMBADA (comparison regime not stated in abstract).
quote: Our experiments show that LT outperforms baseline models on several tasks of machine translation, pre-training, Learning to Execute, and LAMBADA.

title: How Many Layers and Why? An Analysis of the Model Depth in Transformers
claim: In a weight-tied ALBERT with per-token adaptive depth, tokens do not need the same number of iterations, and difficult or task-crucial tokens receive more.
quote: We show that tokens do not require the same amount of iterations and that difficult or crucial tokens for the task are subject to more iterations.

title: How Many Layers and Why? An Analysis of the Model Depth in Transformers
claim: Weight tying lets the encoder stack be read as one transformation iteratively applied, i.e. progressive refinement of token representations.
quote: We interpret the repetition of this application as an iterative process where the token contextualized representations are progressively refined.

title: BERT Loses Patience: Fast and Robust Inference with Early Exit
claim: Overthinking: on ALBERT-base the prediction entropy keeps decreasing with more layers while the actual error rate increases after 10 layers.
quote: Although the model becomes more “confident” (lower entropy indicates higher confidence in BranchyNet [26]) with its prediction as more layers join, the actual error rate instead increases after 10 layers.

title: BERT Loses Patience: Fast and Robust Inference with Early Exit
claim: On ALBERT, patience-based exit improves accuracy over full-depth inference while speeding up inference 1.57x; on BERT accuracy is slightly lower than the original model.
quote: approach consistently improves the performance of the original ALBERT model by a relatively large margin while speeding-up inference by 1.57×.

title: BERT Loses Patience: Fast and Robust Inference with Early Exit
claim: At the same speed-up ratio, PABEE beats confidence/entropy-threshold exits (BranchyNet, Shallow-Deep).
quote: PABEE retains higher accuracy than BranchyNet and Shallow-Deep under the same speed-up ratio, showing its superiority over prediction score based methods.

title: BERT Loses Patience: Fast and Robust Inference with Early Exit
claim: Untied BERT benefits less, which the authors attribute to intermediate layers never having been connected to an output layer during pretraining (train/test mismatch for exits).
quote: We suspect that this is because the intermediate layers of BERT have never been connected to an output layer during pretraining, which leads to a mismatch between pretraining and fine-tuning when adding the internal classifiers.

title: Differentiable Adaptive Computation Time for Visual Reasoning
claim: At similar average computation, DACT-MAC substantially outperforms fixed-step MAC trained with the nearest integer number of steps.
quote: models resulting from the application of DACT to MAC substantially outperform non-adaptive versions of MAC with similar computation cost in the CLEVR dataset

title: Differentiable Adaptive Computation Time for Visual Reasoning
claim: ACT does not respond to its ponder cost on MAC (a variant with zero ponder cost uses 3.2 steps), whereas DACT adapts computation to the penalty.
quote: DACT responds as expected to variations in the ponder cost, adapting its computation accordingly, however, ACT proves to be insensitive to the ponder cost.

title: Differentiable Adaptive Computation Time for Visual Reasoning
claim: Raising the maximum to 15 steps hurts fixed gated MAC but helps DACT fine-tuned from 12-step models, giving the best accuracy (98.72%).
quote: DACT-enabled-MACs with the maximum amount of steps set to 15 can be fine-tuned from existing 12 step models to obtain the best results of any model tested at 98.72% accuracy.

title: Differentiable Adaptive Computation Time for Visual Reasoning
claim: On GQA, where MAC gains little from more than two steps, adding adaptivity slightly reduces accuracy.
quote: Accordingly, adding adaptability to the model does not increase accuracy but rather results in a small but measurable reduction in performance.

title: Comparing Fixed and Adaptive Computation Time for Recurrent Neural Networks
claim: A fixed number of repetitions per token matches ACT on the studied tasks, suggesting ACT's gains come mainly from extra computation rather than adaptivity.
quote: Surprisingly, such uniform distribution of the computational resources matches the performance of ACT in the studied tasks.

title: Comparing Fixed and Adaptive Computation Time for Recurrent Neural Networks
claim: Repeat-RNN solves tasks with fewer training steps and fewer repetitions than ACT, but the right rho is task-dependent (rho = 2 fails on addition).
quote: We observe that in our experiments (1) Repeat-RNN learns how to solve the tasks with less SGD training steps than ACT, and (2) it actually solves them with less repetitions than ACT.

title: Comparing Fixed and Adaptive Computation Time for Recurrent Neural Networks
claim: Too many repetitions destabilize training on addition.
quote: We see that when increasing ρ from 1 performance improves dramatically, but we also observe a limit: with too many repetitions the network shows instabilities with excessively long sequences.

title: Learning to Refine Hidden States for Reliable LLM Reasoning
claim: The refinement depth is chosen per input by an RL-trained controller whose reward is per-step likelihood improvement minus a fixed compute cost.
quote: The controllers are trained with a policy-gradient objective based on step-wise likelihood improvement, enabling input-dependent reasoning control without relying on explicit reasoning.

title: Learning to Refine Hidden States for Reliable LLM Reasoning
claim: Comparisons are to larger 7B baselines and the reward needs ground-truth targets, which the authors list as limitations.
quote: First, our backbone models (LLaMA-1.1B, Gemma-2B, Qwen-3B) are smaller than the 7B baselines in our comparison, which may limit the direct comparability of results.

title: Radial Networks: Dynamic Layer Routing for High-Performance Large Language Models
claim: Per-layer residual contributions are small and shrink with scale, suggesting per-token dynamic depth opportunities.
quote: For example, the residual blocks in the OPT-66B model have a median contribution of 5% to its output.

title: Radial Networks: Dynamic Layer Routing for High-Performance Large Language Models
claim: Radial Networks decouple number of layers from dynamic depth and allow layer reuse via a learned per-token next-layer router; no trained looped results are reported.
quote: They enable scaling to larger model sizes by decoupling the number of layers from the dynamic depth of the network, and their design allows for layer reuse.

title: Depth-Adaptive Graph Recurrent Network for Text Classification
claim: Predicting the depth distribution directly per word (one-shot) is offered as a simpler alternative to ACT's step-wise halting probabilities.
quote: Unlike the continuous layer-wise prediction to determine a stop probability in the ACT, we provide an effective alternative method with more straightforward modeling, which directly predicts the depth distribution among words simultaneously.

title: Adaptive Propagation Graph Convolutional Network
claim: The ponder-style propagation penalty strongly shapes depth on some graphs: a large alpha collapses most nodes to fewer than two steps with GCN-level accuracy, while on high-degree graphs alpha has little effect.
quote: For higher values like α = 0.05, AP-GCN performs mostly less than two propagation steps and the performances are comparable to the GCN reported in Table II. The best value for AP-GCN is found for α = 0.005.

title: N-ODE Transformer: A Depth-Adaptive Variant of the Transformer Using Neural Ordinary Differential Equations
claim: Solver-driven depth adaptivity does not remedy the Transformer's difficulty on PARITY, and penalizing trajectory arclength does not improve accuracy or efficiency.
quote: We find, however, that the depth-adaptivity of the N-ODE Transformer does not provide a remedy for the inherently nonlocal nature of the parity problem, and provide explanations for why this is so.

title: IamNN: Iterative and Adaptive Mobile Neural Network for Efficient Image Classification
claim: ACT plus weight sharing reduces parameters by 90% and computation by 65% on ImageNet, but top-5 drops from 93.3% to 89%; restricting to one iteration per block gives 83.2%.
quote: We are again able to reduce the number of parameters with 90% and the computations by 65% the top5 accuracy drops from 93.3% to 89%.

title: Layer Flexible Adaptive Computational Time
claim: Plain ACT with a single hidden vector gives only marginal benefits over basic RNN/seq2seq, motivating per-layer states.
quote: Our experimental results show that ACT has marginal benefits over basic RNN or sequence to sequence (seq2seq) models, indicating that ACT, with a single hidden vector, cannot always work well.

title: Learning to Reason With Adaptive Computation
claim: ACT's ponder cost is context dependent and difficult to set; optimal settings differed between encoder types.
quote: Additionally, the Ponder Cost parameter shows context dependent behaviour – during preliminary experiments using RNN encoders, the optimal Ponder Cost settings were distinct.

title: Learning to Reason With Adaptive Computation
claim: The adaptive model uses a mean of 5 steps and is both cheaper and better than a large fixed number of steps.
quote: our model takes a mean of 5 steps at inference time, meaning it is both more efficient and performant than using a large, fixed number of steps.

title: Do Language Models Use Their Depth Efficiently?
claim: Layers in the second half of the network contribute much less to the residual stream than those in the first half, with a sharp phase transition near the middle.
quote: layers in the second half contribute much less than those in the first half, with a clear phase transition between the two halves.

title: Do Language Models Use Their Depth Efficiently?
claim: Skipping second-half layers barely affects computations at future token positions, so these layers do not compute reusable sub-results; they refine the current prediction.
quote: the second half of the network barely has any effect on future computations, except for some special layers at the very top of the network.

title: Do Language Models Use Their Depth Efficiently?
claim: The depth of computation (depth score) does not increase with MATH difficulty level or the number of hops in MQuAKE questions.
quote: The depth of computation the model performs is independent of the problem difficulty and the number of hops in the input problem.

title: Do Language Models Use Their Depth Efficiently?
claim: Linear maps from Qwen 2.5 1.5B layers to Qwen 2.5 14B layers show a diagonal pattern: the deeper model is a stretched-out version of the shallow one rather than doing new computation.
quote: This shows that the big model is more likely a “stretched out” version of the shallow model, rather than one that does entirely new computations.

title: Do Language Models Use Their Depth Efficiently?
claim: A shared-layer model (MoEUT) trained from scratch on DeepMind Math uses more of its depth and in a more input-dependent way than a standard Transformer (exploratory, manual study).
quote: MoEUT uses more of its depth, and its depth seems to be more input-dependent.

title: Do Language Models Use Their Depth Efficiently?
claim: The authors argue that if fixed computation depth is caused by the pretraining objective, recurrent latent-thinking methods (they cite the recurrent-depth model, 2502.05171) are fundamentally flawed; if it is architectural, such methods may be the solution.
quote: If the insensitivity of computation depth to input complexity is the consequence of the pretaining objective, such methods are fundamentally flawed.

title: Mixture-of-Depths: Dynamically allocating compute in transformer-based language models
claim: At equal training FLOPs, an MoD transformer can improve the final log-probability objective by up to 1.5% over a vanilla transformer with equal wall-clock training time.
quote: one can train an MoD transformer that improves upon vanilla transformers by as much as 1.5% on the final log probability training objective for equivalent training FLOPs (isoFLOP)

title: Mixture-of-Depths: Dynamically allocating compute in transformer-based language models
claim: MoD models match isoFLOP-optimal baselines while needing a fraction of the FLOPs per forward pass and stepping faster during sampling.
quote: These models match baseline performance for equivalent FLOPS and wall-clock times to train, but require a fraction of the FLOPs per forward pass, and can be upwards of 50% faster to step during post-training sampling.

title: Mixture-of-Depths: Dynamically allocating compute in transformer-based language models
claim: The best configuration routes every other block with 12.5% capacity; learned routing is essential, stochastic routing is drastically worse.
quote: We found that it is best to use 12.5% capacity blocks, every other block.

title: Mixture-of-Depths: Dynamically allocating compute in transformer-based language models
claim: Learned routing is crucial: stochastic (Gaussian-sampled) top-k routing performs drastically worse than both the baseline and learned-routing MoD.
quote: Learned routing is crucial, as MoD transformers that use stochastic routing

title: Mixture-of-Depths: Dynamically allocating compute in transformer-based language models
claim: When adding FLOPs to an MoD model, adding depth is better than adding width.
quote: Empirically, we find that it is better to add depth than to add width when adding FLOPs to the model.

title: Mixture-of-Depths: Dynamically allocating compute in transformer-based language models
claim: Gains from MoD compound with Mixture-of-Experts (MoDE), and integrated no-op experts beat simply reducing expert capacity.
quote: In figure 7 we present results showing that the performance improvments offered by MoD compound with those of MoE.

title: A Survey on Latent Reasoning
claim: The survey's top-level taxonomy splits latent CoT into vertical recurrence (expanding computational depth) and horizontal recurrence (expanding sequential capacity).
quote: These categories can be broadly divided into two types: 1) vertical recurrence for expanding computational depth, and 2) horizontal recurrence for increasing sequential capacity.

title: A Survey on Latent Reasoning
claim: Explicit CoT transmits about 15 bits per step while a 2560-d FP16 hidden state carries about 40,960 bits, a bandwidth gap of roughly three orders of magnitude (motivation for latent reasoning).
quote: exchanges full 2560-dimensional FP16 hidden states (≈ 40, 960 bits each), revealing a ∼ 2.7 × 103 fold bandwidth gap between the two approaches.

title: A Survey on Latent Reasoning
claim: Recent looped architectures (Recursive Transformer, AlgoFormer, recurrent-depth) have converged on a Prelude/Loop/Coda structure.
quote: recent architectures like Recursive Transformer [2], AlgoFormer [29], and Recurrent-Depth [31] have converged on a three-stage Pre/Loop/Coda structure.

title: A Survey on Latent Reasoning
claim: The survey reads a trend from complex adaptive halting (ACT) to simple fixed or convergence-based stopping, and concludes adaptive mechanisms may not be worth their overhead (an interpretive claim, not tested).
quote: This evolution suggests that complex adaptive mechanisms may not justify their computational overhead in practice.

title: A Survey on Latent Reasoning
claim: Training-induced recurrence (Coconut, CODI, CCoT, pause/filler tokens) is framed as complementary to architectural looping.
quote: The relationship between these training-induced methods and architectural recurrence is complementary rather than competitive.

title: A Survey on Latent Reasoning
claim: The survey explicitly does not compare methods empirically and notes most studies compare to non-reasoning baselines rather than to each other.
quote: Furthermore, most studies compare their models to non-reasoning LLM baselines rather than to each other.

title: A Survey on Latent Reasoning
claim: Diffusion language models are framed as 'spatial infinite-depth reasoning' via iterative parallel denoising with adjustable step counts.
quote: Spatial infinite-depth reasoning is realized by diffusion models that begin with a fully masked or noisy draft of the entire output and iteratively denoise it in parallel

title: A Survey on Latent Reasoning
claim: Gradient-state recurrent models (TTT, Titans, Atlas) are framed as trading sequence length for depth: each token is an optimizer step on a fast-weight layer.
quote: processing a longer sequence is mathematically equivalent to running the same layer for more optimization iterations, thereby yielding greater reasoning depth without adding parameters.

title: Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
claim: With 6 continuous thoughts, Coconut reaches 34.1% on GSM8k vs 16.5% for no-CoT (same GPT-2 base), but stays below language CoT (42.9%).
quote: by using 6 continuous thoughts, Coconut achieves 34.1% accuracy on GSM8k, which significantly outperforms No-CoT (16.5%).

title: Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
claim: Coconut does not surpass CoT on GSM8k but gives a better accuracy/generated-token trade-off.
quote: Although Coconut does not surpass CoT on GSM8k, it offers a superior trade-off between reasoning efficiency and accuracy (Figure 8, I).

title: Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
claim: Continuous thoughts can encode multiple candidate next steps, yielding BFS-like latent search on planning-heavy logical tasks where Coconut outperforms CoT.
quote: continuous thoughts can encode multiple alternative next steps, allowing the model to perform a breadth-first search (BFS) rather than committing prematurely to a single deterministic path as in CoT

title: Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
claim: Without the multi-stage language-CoT curriculum, Coconut is no better than no-CoT: latent reasoning still needs language supervision to learn.
quote: we found the models trained this way do not perform any better than no-CoT

title: Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
claim: On Llama 3.2-3B and Llama 3-8B, Coconut gains over no-CoT are consistent but smaller than at GPT-2 scale.
quote: We observe consistent performance gains across both Llama 3.2-3B and Llama 3-8B models compared to the no-CoT baseline, though these improvements are not as pronounced as those previously demonstrated

title: Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
claim: Training requires n+1 sequential forward passes for n latent thoughts, which limits parallelism; adding 3 thoughts per step at once causes loss spikes and instability.
quote: adding three continuous thoughts at once – particularly during the final stage transition – leads to a sharp spike in training loss, causing instability.

title: State Stream Transformer (SST) V2: Parallel Training of Nonlinear Recurrence for Latent Space Reasoning
claim: Co-training the state stream into a 27B backbone on a small GSM8K set gives +15.15 points on GPQA-Diamond over a fine-tuning-matched baseline.
quote: Co-trained into an existing 27B backbone using only a small dataset of GSM8K examples, the SST delivers a +15.15 point gain over a fine-tuning-matched baseline on out-of-distribution GPQA-Diamond

title: State Stream Transformer (SST) V2: Parallel Training of Nonlinear Recurrence for Latent Space Reasoning
claim: The same recurrence supports per-position latent deliberation at inference, spending extra FLOPs before committing to a token.
quote: This same mechanism supports continuous latent deliberation per position at inference time, dedicating additional FLOPs to exploring abstract reasoning before committing to a token.

title: Trading Depth for Time in Recurrent Transformers
claim: An L-layer LRT with one thought token comes within 0.006/0.004 bits per byte of a 2L-layer LRT, recovering 67%/81% of the improvement with about 48% fewer parameters.
quote: one thought token brings the shallower model within 0.006 and 0.004 bits per byte of its double-depth counterpart, recovering 67% and 81% of the improvement with approximately 48% fewer total parameters.

title: Trading Depth for Time in Recurrent Transformers
claim: The comparison is controlled: both models execute 2L blocks per vocabulary token during decoding; only parameter count differs.
quote: Both execute $2L$ Transformer blocks per vocabulary token during decoding, but the thought-token model uses fewer parameters.

title: Recursive Multi-Agent Systems
claim: The paper frames looped/recursive LMs as a scaling axis and extends recursion from one model to a multi-agent system.
quote: Recursive or looped language models have recently emerged as a new scaling axis by iteratively refining the same model computation over latent states to deepen reasoning.

title: Recursive Multi-Agent Systems
claim: Across 9 benchmarks RecursiveMAS improves average accuracy by 8.3% with 1.2x-2.4x speedup and 34.6%-75.6% token reduction vs single/multi-agent and recursive baselines.
quote: RecursiveMAS consistently delivers an average accuracy improvement of 8.3%, together with 1.2$\times$-2.4$\times$ end-to-end inference speedup, and 34.6%-75.6% token usage reduction.

title: Recirculation
claim: The authors distinguish recirculation from chain-of-thought and from depth-recurrence (looping).
quote: We distinguish this technique from chain-of-thought computation---which is better reserved for complex inferences rather than basic state tracking---as well as from popular depth-recurrence techniques (looping) and the costly training of recurrent transformers.

title: Recirculation
claim: Adaptive recirculation on frozen Gemma3 models reduces perplexity and gives a 21% relative GSM8k accuracy increase over the off-the-shelf baseline.
quote: adaptive recirculation achieves surprising gains on the Gemma3 family, including a consistent reduction in perplexity on a suite of datasets, a 21% increase in relative accuracy on GSM8k

title: Emergent Search and Backtracking in Latent Reasoning Models
claim: Backtracking in latent deliberation occurs in 32% of instances and is associated with a 34% accuracy gain over non-backtracking instances.
quote: Backtracking is prevalent (32% of instances), beneficial (34% accuracy gain over non-backtracking instances), and predominantly directed away from the semantically closest distractor toward the correct answer.

title: Emergent Search and Backtracking in Latent Reasoning Models
claim: Latent search is adaptive: implausible distractors shorten exploration by 54%.
quote: The search is adaptive: replacing distractors with implausible alternatives shortens exploration by 54%.

title: Temporal Recurrence Favors Fewer Layers
claim: Temporal recurrence shifts the best compute allocation toward substantially fewer layers per step with comparable or better performance.
quote: Across Sokoban and autoregressive FineWeb language modeling, we find that temporal recurrence shifts the best observed compute allocation toward substantially fewer layers, with comparable or better performance.

title: Temporal Recurrence Favors Fewer Layers
claim: The comparison is between best observed recurrent and non-recurrent allocations under approximately matched per-step computation across budgets.
quote: For each budget, we compare the best observed recurrent and non-recurrent allocations and the performance they achieve under approximately matched per-step computation.

title: Not All Thinking is Created Equal: Latent Reasoning Discovers a Recurrent Search Algorithm for Depth Generalization
claim: Vanilla, CoT and pause-token models do well in distribution but generalize poorly to longer-hop OOD problems.
quote: Vanilla, CoT, and Pause Token models solve ID problems well, but rely largely on local graph features and generalize poorly to out-of-distribution (OOD) problems with longer hops.

title: Not All Thinking is Created Equal: Latent Reasoning Discovers a Recurrent Search Algorithm for Depth Generalization
claim: Latent recurrence learns a reusable forward-search algorithm that generalizes beyond the training depth.
quote: In this setting, latent recurrence supports a reusable forward-search algorithm that generalizes beyond the training depth.

title: Not All Thinking is Created Equal: Latent Reasoning Discovers a Recurrent Search Algorithm for Depth Generalization
claim: Circuit analysis localizes a sparse recurrent search circuit: an attention head retrieves relations and the MLP/residual update the reachability state across recurrent steps.
quote: an attention head retrieves graph relations, an MLP and the residual stream update the reachability state across recurrent steps, while multiple attention heads together then do the candidate matching.

title: Hidden Decoding at Scale: Latent Computation Scaling for Large Language Models
claim: The authors argue looped Transformers are hard to scale because looped computation conflicts with pipeline parallelism, motivating sequence-length scaling instead.
quote: Depth-recurrent (looped) Transformers pursue this goal but are hard to scale, because looped computation does not fit naturally with the pipeline parallelism used to train the largest models.

title: Hidden Decoding at Scale: Latent Computation Scaling for Large Language Models
claim: WeLM-HD4-80B and WeLM-HD4-617B (n=4) improve their matched non-HD baselines, the first sequence-length scaling demonstration at 100B+ MoE scale.
quote: At frontier scale, we train WeLM-HD4-80B and WeLM-HD4-617B at n=4 and improve their matched non-HD baselines, making Hidden Decoding the first demonstrated sequence-length scaling method at the 100B+ MoE scale.

title: Hidden Decoding at Scale: Latent Computation Scaling for Large Language Models
claim: Gains grow with the expansion factor n.
quote: Across expansion factors, the gains grow as n increases, showing that sequence-length expansion is a practical fixed-backbone scaling path for frontier-scale LLMs.

title: N-vium: Mixture-of-Exits Transformer for Accelerated Exact Generation
claim: The largest N-vium model achieves a 57.9% wall-clock speedup over a parameter- and data-matched Transformer without perplexity loss.
quote: Our largest model reaches 57.9% wall-clock speedup over a parameter- and data-matched standard transformer at no perplexity cost.

title: N-vium: Mixture-of-Exits Transformer for Accelerated Exact Generation
claim: The mixture-of-exits formulation strictly generalizes the standard Transformer.
quote: This formulation strictly generalizes the standard transformer, which is recovered exactly when routing assigns zero mass to all intermediate heads.

title: The Illusion of Superposition? A Principled Analysis of Latent Thinking in Language Models
claim: In training-free and fine-tuned latent-CoT regimes superposition collapses or is unused, and models find shortcuts.
quote: In the training-free and fine-tuned regimes, we find that the superposition either collapses or is not used at all, with models discovering shortcut solutions instead.

title: The Illusion of Superposition? A Principled Analysis of Latent Thinking in Language Models
claim: Two causes are proposed: language pretraining biases late layers to commit to a token, and capacity shapes which solution is favored.
quote: i) pretraining on natural language data biases models to commit to a token in the last layers ii) capacity has a huge effect on which solutions a model favors

title: Inverse Depth Scaling From Most Layers Being Similar
claim: Loss scales inversely proportional to depth, probably because functionally similar layers reduce error by ensemble averaging.
quote: We find loss scales inversely proportional to depth in LLMs, probably due to functionally similar layers reducing error through ensemble averaging rather than compositional learning or discretizing smooth dynamics.

title: Inverse Depth Scaling From Most Layers Being Similar
claim: The authors conclude that efficiency gains may need architectures that encourage compositional use of depth.
quote: The findings suggest that improving LLM efficiency may require architectural innovations to encourage compositional use of depth.

title: PonderLM-3: Adaptive Token-Wise Pondering with Differentiable Masking
claim: At equal inference FLOPs, PonderLM-3 has lower pretraining perplexity than existing recursive or adaptive baselines.
quote: compared with existing recursive or adaptive baselines, it achieves lower pretraining perplexity at equal inference FLOPs.

title: PonderLM-3: Adaptive Token-Wise Pondering with Differentiable Masking
claim: Downstream, it matches fixed-step PonderLM-2 at the same maximum number of extra steps while using fewer inference FLOPs.
quote: PonderLM-3 attains comparable performance to fixed-step PonderLM-2 under the same maximum number of additional computation steps, while using fewer inference FLOPs in practice.

title: Full-bandwidth transformer
claim: Latent feedback lets 1B models match or approach standard Transformers trained with about 1.5x more tokens, with negligible decoding overhead.
quote: With negligible per-token decoding overhead, full-bandwidth transformers match or approach standard transformers trained with roughly 1.5x more tokens, and manage to produce shorter reasoning when no off-policy templates are provided.

title: Full-bandwidth transformer
claim: Mechanism: the previous top-layer hidden state is fused with the sampled token embedding via a gated linear unit and fed back as input.
quote: at each decoding step, the previous top-layer hidden state is fused with the sampled token embedding through a gated linear unit and fed back as the next input.

title: Do Transformers Use their Depth Adaptively? Evidence from a Relational Reasoning Task
claim: Pretrained models show only limited adaptive depth use: some larger models need fewer layers for easier tasks.
quote: For pretrained models, we find some limited evidence for adaptive depth use: some larger models need fewer layers to arrive at plausible answers for easier tasks

title: Do Transformers Use their Depth Adaptively? Evidence from a Relational Reasoning Task
claim: Finetuned models show clearer adaptive depth use, more so under less constrained finetuning.
