quote: For our experiments, we replicated the TRM experiments and achieved slightly lower results than those reported in the original paper.

title: Reasoning with Neural Cellular Automata
claim: Strictly local NCAs solve complex multi-step reasoning tasks with compact architectures.
quote: On all the evaluated visual reasoning benchmarks (Mazes, Sudoku, ARC-AGI-1), NCAs demonstrate strong accuracy using a highly compact, local architecture with few parameters (Table 1).

title: Reasoning with Neural Cellular Automata
claim: Parallel stochastic rollouts raise ARC-AGI-1 pass@2 from 28.25% to 48.75%; pass@64 reaches 60.3%, showing candidate selection is a bottleneck.
quote: In ARC-AGI-1, the use of parallel stochastic rollouts from different augmented inputs similarly increases pass@2 performances on the evaluation set from 28.25% (K=1, D=64) to 48.75% (K=3264, D=64).

title: Reasoning with Neural Cellular Automata
claim: Generalization depends on sample replay, perturbations and asynchronous updates during training.
quote: We find that training perturbations combined with sample replay act as critical regularizers during training to achieve generalization (Figure 7A).

title: Reasoning with Neural Cellular Automata
claim: At fixed FLOPs on Sudoku-Extreme, reallocating compute to depth with pruning beats breadth in low-compute regimes.
quote: Similarly, at equivalent FLOP budgets, deeper rollouts compressed via pruning outperform standard baselines in compute-constrained regimes: at a base budget 𝐷base = 64, quadrupling depth ( 𝐷 = 256, 𝑚 = 8) boosts accuracy from 25.6% to 81.7% (Figure 6B).

title: Equilibrium Reasoners: Learning Attractors Enables Scalable Reasoning
claim: Weight-tying beats a feedforward stack at the same number of layer evaluations on Sudoku-Extreme (32.6% vs 2.6%) with 5.03M vs 105.6M parameters; the feedforward model memorizes (93.8% train).
quote: Feedforward models do not induce such refinement trajectories; in our controlled comparison, they generalize substantially worse than iterative alternatives in Tab. 1.

title: Equilibrium Reasoners: Learning Attractors Enables Scalable Reasoning
claim: Training with randomized initial states and noise injection improves accuracy at the same inference budget, most on Maze-Unique.
quote: In Tab. 3, the full RI+NI training improves Sudoku from 84.8 to 86.4 and Maze from 44.9 to 82.2, with RI alone already raising Maze accuracy to 68.6.

title: Equilibrium Reasoners: Learning Attractors Enables Scalable Reasoning
claim: Depth and breadth test-time scaling compound: Sudoku 86.4 to 93.0 (D 16 to 64) to 99.8 (B=128); Maze 82.2 to 88.9 to 93.0.
quote: Tab. 4 makes this effect explicit: at B=1, increasing the depth from D=16 to D=64 raises EqR from 86.4 to 93.0 on Sudoku and from 82.2 to 88.9 on Maze.

title: Equilibrium Reasoners: Learning Attractors Enables Scalable Reasoning
claim: Hierarchical (two-latent) iteration and ACT interact with the recipe: with learned ACT the hierarchical model reaches 84.8% vs 73.9% for single-latent; oracle halting collapses training.
quote: With learned ACT, the hierarchical latent model reaches 84.8% on Sudoku, while the corresponding single-latent z variant reaches 73.9%.

title: Equilibrium Reasoners: Learning Attractors Enables Scalable Reasoning
claim: On Mini-ARC EqR beats HRM and TRM.
quote: On Mini-ARC, EqR reaches 55.28% exact accuracy, improving over both HRM (44.85%) and TRM (48.35%).

title: Diffusion as a Training Curriculum for Timestep-Free Iterative Reasoning
claim: Inference depth is a free compute axis: solve rate rises monotonically to K=10,000 steps although gradients only span 4-step segments.
quote: Additional recurrent steps keep solving previously unsolved instances, so inference depth becomes a free compute axis: gradients through four-step truncated segments suffice to reach 99.90% solve rate at 𝐾 =10,000 denoising steps on Sudoku-Extreme and 98.93% on Maze-Unique at 𝐾 = 100.

title: Diffusion as a Training Curriculum for Timestep-Free Iterative Reasoning
claim: Progressive denoising is unnecessary at inference; constant maximal noise is best, and removing noise collapses performance.
quote: As stochasticity is reduced, performance falls monotonically, reaching 49.39% when we propagate the clean prediction between denoising steps without any noise injection (𝑡 = 1.00).

title: Diffusion as a Training Curriculum for Timestep-Free Iterative Reasoning
claim: The annealed-corruption training curriculum is what matters: fixed-noise or clean-only training degrade sharply.
quote: Performing training with fixed non-annealed noise, or removing noise completely significantly degrades performance to 82.73% and 0.00%, respectively (Supp. Tab. 2).

title: Diffusion as a Training Curriculum for Timestep-Free Iterative Reasoning
claim: On Maze-Hard the strict exact metric is below TRM's reported number, optimal-path metric on par.
quote: The strict exact metric on Maze-Hard (77.87% at 𝐾 =100) sits a few points below TRM’s reported 85.3%, while the multi-path optimal metric (86.43%) is on par.

title: Think Deep, Speak Once: Relit, A Recursive Latent Implicit Transformer Framework
claim: A recursive block on a frozen 1.1B LM matches or beats much larger few-shot LLMs on ProofWriter and RuleTaker.
quote: Empirically, ReLIT achieves high parameter efficiency on the GLoRE logical reasoning benchmark, matching or outperforming significantly larger models on challenging tasks such as ProofWriter and RuleTaker despite minimal supervision.

title: Think Deep, Speak Once: Relit, A Recursive Latent Implicit Transformer Framework
claim: Halting depth grows with task difficulty / data scarcity (3.6 steps ProofWriter, 5.2 RuleTaker, 7.8 NaN-NLI).
quote: For this dataset, the average halting depth increases to 5.2 steps. This slightly higher value reflects the increased complexity of the rules, requiring the ReLIT-Block to perform additional residual updates to reach a stable logical fixed point.

title: Think Deep, Speak Once: Relit, A Recursive Latent Implicit Transformer Framework
claim: Recursion over a frozen anchor cannot add information absent from the backbone features (data processing inequality bottleneck).
quote: This formulation reveals a critical limitation: regardless of the recursive depth, the reasoning capacity of Fθ is restricted to transforming and reparameterizing the information already present in x.

title: Energy-guided Recursive Model
claim: With D<=64 and K=128, energy selection matches candidate-pool oracle accuracy on Sudoku, PPBench and Maze.
quote: With D ≤ 64 and K = 128, ERM matches the evaluated candidate-pool oracles on Sudoku, PPBench, and Maze, and supports early stopping.

title: Energy-guided Recursive Model
claim: Learned q-head halting and confidence saturate and select worse candidates on Maze than the rule energy.
quote: On Maze, ERM reaches the 99.30% oracle, compared with 97.80% for majority and confidence and 97.30% for q-head.

title: Energy-guided Recursive Model
claim: Deeper recurrence does not guarantee better accuracy; energy-based stopping uses far fewer steps.
quote: With K = 128 PT replicas and a maximum depth of 64, all 63 batches stop by this criterion at depths 6–11, averaging 7.60 steps, with 996/1000 = 99.60% exact accuracy (Table 4).

title: Energy-guided Recursive Model
claim: Hopfield continuation memory reduces perplexity of a fixed recurrent EBT, without establishing any advantage over a non-recurrent Transformer++.
quote: ERM reduces perplexity from 44.189 to 43.419 (Table 3), a 1.742% improvement (paired-document bootstrap 95% CI: 1.711–1.773%), and improves on candidate averaging by 1.649%.

title: Recursive Inference Machines for Neural Reasoning
claim: Non-identity reweighters (RIMA, RIMformer) outperform TRM (identity reweighter) on symbolic benchmarks.
quote: We observe that the RIMs with non-trivial Reweighters (RIMFormer and RIMA) consistently outperform the identity-reweighted RIM (SimRIM).

title: Recursive Inference Machines for Neural Reasoning
claim: Fully dynamic (learned, input-dependent) reweighting beats static EMA coefficients, which hurt TRM on Sudoku-Extreme.
quote: The results indicate that fully dynamic, neuraldriven reweighting consistently yields superior performance, suggesting that joint adaptation of both latent trajectories is essential for solving high-complexity reasoning tasks.

title: Recursive Inference Machines for Neural Reasoning
claim: Longer lookback (attention over history) helps Maze-Hard but hurts Sudoku-Extreme.
quote: We observe that increasing the lookback window size does not yield better performance in all cases. While it improves performance on Maze-Hard, it reduces performance on Sudoku-Extreme.

title: Stream Recursion Model (SRM)
claim: SRM-base matches GPT-2 loss with about half the parameters but about 7x the training time; SRM-med beats GPT-2 at similar parameters with about 6x compute.
quote: We see that SRM-base is able to achieve on par performance to GPT-2 with roughly half the parameters and 7 times the compute time.

title: Stream Recursion Model (SRM)
claim: HRM as originally designed fails on language modeling.
quote: We demonstrated that HRM, as it was originally designed was incapable of performing on language datasets.

title: Stream Recursion Model (SRM)
claim: Backprop through more than 4 of 8 recursive layers gives diminishing returns.
quote: Using a fixed depth of 8 layers we found that returns severely diminished when performing backpropagation through more than 4 layers.

title: Dynamical Systems Theory Behind a Hierarchical Reasoning Model
claim: A 5M CMM reaches 93.7% on Sudoku-Extreme, above HRM (55.0%) and TRM (87.4%) as reported in their papers.
quote: On the Sudoku-Extreme benchmark, a 5M-parameter CMM achieves a state-of-the-art accuracy of 93.7%, outperforming the 27M-parameter HRM (55.0%) and 5M-parameter TRM (87.4%).

title: Dynamical Systems Theory Behind a Hierarchical Reasoning Model
claim: Re-running HRM and TRM under a 16 GB / AMP budget lowers their Sudoku-Extreme accuracy, while TRM Maze reproduces.
quote: While the reproduced TRM results for the Maze benchmark closely match the originally reported metrics, a noticeable performance drop is observed in the Sudoku-Extreme reproduction for both HRM and TRM.

title: Dynamical Systems Theory Behind a Hierarchical Reasoning Model
claim: Weight-sharing across recursive steps halves the tiny model to 0.26M parameters while retaining 85.4% Sudoku-Extreme and 82.2% Maze.
quote: Remarkably, even when aggressively compressed to an ultra-tiny footprint of just 0.26M parameters, the CMM retains robust predictive power, achieving 85.4% on Sudoku-Extreme and 82.2% on the Maze benchmark.

title: Dynamical Systems Theory Behind a Hierarchical Reasoning Model
claim: Noise injection (NSDE) broadens the basin of attraction and counters overfitting of deterministic recursion.
quote: The injection of noise creates a robust manifold of initial states, forcing the system to learn a broader basin of attraction towards the stable equilibrium.

title: Tiny Recursive Reasoning with Mamba-2 Attention Hybrid
claim: At parameter parity, the Mamba-2 hybrid improves ARC-AGI-1 pass@2 by 2.0 points with pass@1 parity.
quote: On ARCAGI-1, we find that the hybrid improves pass@2 (the official metric) by +2.0% (45.88% vs 43.88%) and consistently outperforms at higher K values (+4.75% at pass@100), whilst maintaining pass@1 parity.

title: Tiny Recursive Reasoning with Mamba-2 Attention Hybrid
claim: Operator choice is task dependent: MLP-t mixing best on Sudoku, fails completely on 30x30 Maze where the hybrid beats attention.
quote: Maze (Table 3): In contrast to Sudoku, both MLP-t variants completely fail on the larger 30×30 grids (0.0% accuracy), whilst TR-mamba2attn achieves 80.6% versus 60.8% for TRM-attn.

title: Tiny Recursive Reasoning with Mamba-2 Attention Hybrid
claim: Post-norm is needed for stability of unrolled recursion, independent of HRM's Q-learning motivation.
quote: We argue that post-norm is essential for recursion stability itself, independent of Qlearning: it bounds the residual stream magnitude across recursive unrolling, preventing divergence.

title: Structured Sparse Memory for Recurrent Reasoning
claim: The task-embedding table, excluded from usual model-size counts, is an order of magnitude larger than the recurrent backbone in HRM/TRM/URM.
quote: In existing XRM systems, the task embedding table can be more than 30 times larger than the backbone itself: ∼448M learnable parameters on ARC-AGI-1 and ∼610M on ARC-AGI-2.

title: Structured Sparse Memory for Recurrent Reasoning
claim: At matched forward and backward FLOPs, more recurrence with fewer unique layers beats more unique layers (which overfit), up to a point; intermediate gradient horizons are best.
quote: At matched forward and backward FLOPs, too many unique layers overfit while too few provide insufficient capacity. At fixed forward configuration, intermediate learning horizons outperform both very short and full horizons.

title: Structured Sparse Memory for Recurrent Reasoning
claim: Matched synthetic data outweighs recurrent architectural choices, especially on ARC-AGI-2.
quote: In our experiments, this matched synthetic data is the largest measured driver of ARC-AGI-2 gains.

title: Structured Sparse Memory for Recurrent Reasoning
claim: XRM evaluation lets training use the public-evaluation demonstration pairs (but not held-out outputs).
quote: We follow the XRM evaluation setup, where public-evaluation training pairs are available during training but held-out outputs are not.

title: Boosting Inference with Guided Reasoning: Stochastic Exploration for Recursive Models
claim: Guided stochastic exploration raises Sudoku-Extreme exact solve from 85.9% to 98.0% without retraining.
quote: On Sudoku-Extreme (Wang et al., 2025), our method improves exact-solve accuracy from 85.9±0.6% to 98.0±0.3%, solving previously out-of-reach failure cases and recovering baseline performance at much lower depths (Figure 1).

title: Boosting Inference with Guided Reasoning: Stochastic Exploration for Recursive Models
claim: On Maze-Hard exploration exposes headroom but the Q-head guide is too flat to exploit it; the diagnostics predict this without labels.
quote: On Maze-Hard exploration is stable but the Q-head guide is too flat: the spread bound flags this label-free, a priori (Figure 3), and evaluation confirms the predicted non-improvement (Table 1).

title: Boosting Inference with Guided Reasoning: Stochastic Exploration for Recursive Models
claim: Recursive models leave trajectory-level headroom that requires both stable exploration and an aligned internal guide.
quote: The lesson is that recursive models leave useful trajectory-level headroom, but recovering it requires both stable exploration and a ranking-aligned internal guide.

title: Flow Reasoning Models: Turning Flows Into Efficient Recurrent Reasoners
claim: FRM matches EqR's peak Sudoku-Extreme solve rate with 44x fewer inference FLOPs and reaches higher peak accuracy.
quote: On Sudoku-Extreme, FRMs reach a peak solve rate of 99.5% and match EqR’s peak 98.7% solve rate (Huang et al., 2026) with 44× fewer inference FLOPs (Figure 1).

title: Flow Reasoning Models: Turning Flows Into Efficient Recurrent Reasoners
claim: Plain self-conditioning converges to confidently incorrect fixed points; Fixed-Point Forcing turns extra recurrent depth into accuracy.
quote: Replacing the one-pass training carry with a rollout-derived carry raises the three-seed mean solve rate from 32.6% to 99.2% on Sudoku-Extreme and from 96.2% to 98.0% on Maze-Unique.

title: Flow Reasoning Models: Turning Flows Into Efficient Recurrent Reasoners
claim: Under FPF, convergence residual becomes a near-perfect correctness signal (AUROC 1.00 vs 0.50).
quote: This residual changes from a chance-level correctness signal under conventional self-conditioning to a nearly perfect one under FPF (AUROC 1.00; Fig. 6c).

title: Compute Time Scaling with Recursive Models for Combinatorial Optimization
claim: TRM4CO reaches the lowest optimality gap among learned solvers on TSP-500 and TSP-1000.
quote: Empirically, TRM4CO reaches the lowest optimality gap of all learned solvers on TSP-500 and TSP-1000, e.g. 0.11% on TSP-500 in 2.1 seconds per instance, and matches the best diffusion solver on TSP-10000.

title: Compute Time Scaling with Recursive Models for Combinatorial Optimization
claim: For MIS, width (parallel rollouts) matters more than depth; depth gives a small consistent gain only with fine peeling.
quote: On ER-[700-800], width matters more than depth. At kp = 8 the gap falls steadily with K, while the curves for D ∈ {16, 32} lie on top of each other.

title: Compute Time Scaling with Recursive Models for Combinatorial Optimization
claim: Self-relabeling without supervision from near-optimal solutions yields comparable quality.
quote: Self-relabeling can, while forgoing supervision from near-optimal solutions, still result in on-par quality.

title: Steering Recurrent Reasoners at Inference Time with Readout Feedback
claim: RoFB improves four of six model-task pairs at the same or lower compute, reaching accuracies unattainable by more steps or more voted trajectories.
quote: Across three recurrent models (AKOrN, ItrSA++, TRM) on Sudoku and Maze, RoFB yields clear gains in four of six model-task pairs, achieving performance unattainable by merely running more steps or selecting from multiple trajectories, at comparable or lower computational cost.

title: Steering Recurrent Reasoners at Inference Time with Readout Feedback
claim: For TRM on Sudoku-Extreme (no voting possible because TRM uses a fixed initial latent), RoFB adds 5.8 points; on Maze-Hard it is null.
quote: For TRM on Sudoku, where confidence-based voting is unavailable, RoFB lifts board accuracy from 68.4% to 74.2% (+5.8%) at Nblock =16, demonstrating that the gain does not depend on the availability of a voting mechanism.

title: One Step Forward and K Steps Back: Better Reasoning with Denoising Recursion Models
claim: Non-recursive Transformers at matched compute are far below TRM on ARC-Easy; diffusion without recursive backprop fails.
quote: A standard transformer achieved only 25.5% on ARC-Easy, far below the recursive TRM baseline of 45.7%. Crucially, we found that diffusion without backpropagating through multiple recursive steps performs very poorly.

title: One Step Forward and K Steps Back: Better Reasoning with Denoising Recursion Models
claim: DRM beats TRM on ARC2-Eval at equal parameters and data, including with large pretraining.
quote: Even in the high-data regime (NVARC pretraining), DRM improved ARC2-Eval accuracy from 12.5% to 16.7% (7M params) and 21.8% to 24.9% (14M params).

title: One Step Forward and K Steps Back: Better Reasoning with Denoising Recursion Models
claim: Removing deep supervision from TRM costs 11 points on ARC-Easy, whereas DRM needs none.
quote: When we removed this supervision (“TRM w/o deep sup”), performance fell by 11% (from 45.7% to 34.7%) on ARC-Easy.

title: One Step Forward and K Steps Back: Better Reasoning with Denoising Recursion Models
claim: Backpropagating through a window of recursions is the core ingredient of these small models.
quote: These findings suggest that the core ingredient to the success of these small models is backpropagating through a window of recursions.

title: One Step Forward and K Steps Back: Better Reasoning with Denoising Recursion Models
claim: DRM is much worse than TRM on Sudoku, attributed to long sequential dependencies.
quote: On Sudoku, DRM achieved 20% accuracy compared to 87.9% for TRM.

title: Generative Recursive Reasoning
claim: With 20 parallel samples at 16 iterations GRAM beats deterministic baselines run for 320 iterations, at comparable compute.
quote: Notably, GRAM with N = 20 samples at 16 iterations outperforms all deterministic baselines at 320 iterations, including TRM (97.0% vs 90.5%), despite comparable computational budget.

title: Generative Recursive Reasoning
claim: Deterministic recursive models cannot represent multiple solutions (coverage at most 36.1%).
quote: Table 1 reveals that deterministic recursive models structurally cannot capture multiple solutions, with coverage at most 36.1% across all tasks.

title: Generative Recursive Reasoning
claim: Stochastic guidance helps across architectures; stochasticity and learned guidance are both needed.
quote: For (b), both stochasticity and learned guidance are essential—removing either significantly degrades performance.

title: Generative Recursive Reasoning
claim: Data augmentation and parallel sampling are complementary: with heavy augmentation, extra samples stop helping on ARC-AGI-1.
quote: At Aug=50, performance saturates regardless of sample count—accuracy remains nearly constant whether we draw 1 or 50 samples.

title: Channel-Wise MLPs Improve the Generalization of Recurrent Convolutional Networks
claim: Adding a channel-wise gated MLP to a recurrent convolution improves ID and especially OOD exact-match generalization at matched parameters.
quote: Using the Re-ARC benchmark as our testbed, we show that DAMP achieves a median accuracy of 92.19% on in-distribution tasks compared to DARC’s 78.75%, and more remarkably, 14.58% on out-of-distribution tasks compared to DARC’s 2.34%, in a parameter-matched setting.

title: Test-time Adaptation of Tiny Recursive Models
claim: A pre-trained TRM can be efficiently fine-tuned on competition tasks within compute limits, reaching 6.67% on the ARC-AGI-2 semi-private set.
quote: That model was then post-trained in just 12,500 gradient steps during the competition to reach a score of 6.67% on semi-private evaluation tasks.

title: Test-time Adaptation of Tiny Recursive Models
claim: Full fine-tuning of the tiny model beats LoRA or embedding-only fine-tuning.
quote: Notably, such post-training performance is achieved by full fine tuning of the tiny model, not LoRA fine-tuning or fine-tuning of task embeddings alone.

title: Slots, Transitions, Loops: Learning Composable World Models for ARC
claim: Loop-OWM outperforms non-looped and looped baselines with comparable or fewer parameters on ARC-1 and ARC-2.
quote: On both ARC-1 and ARC-2, Loop-OWM outperforms non-looped and looped baselines with comparable or fewer parameters.

title: Slots, Transitions, Loops: Learning Composable World Models for ARC
claim: Individual loop steps do not acquire stable, interpretable semantics.
quote: Although Loop-OWM uses recurrence as a rollout mechanism, we do not observe stable, humaninterpretable semantics at individual loop steps, as shown in Figure 3.

title: Winfree Oscillatory Neural Network
claim: WONN beats HRM on Maze-hard with 1.47% of HRM's parameters; energy voting adds about 4 points.
quote: Despite using only 0.396M parameters (1.47% of HRM), WONN achieves 76.2% accuracy.

title: Not Too Hard, Not Too Easy: Learning from Intermediate States for LLM Structured Reasoning
claim: Frontier-state curation greatly improves a recurrent updater on top of an LLM versus training only on final answers.
quote: With Qwen3-1.7B, FOCUS achieves 64.4% exact accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme and 91.1% on MazeHard, compared with 7.2% and 86.0% for Recurrent final-only.

title: Not Too Hard, Not Too Easy: Learning from Intermediate States for LLM Structured Reasoning
claim: The Sudoku-trained adapter transfers zero-shot to math and code reasoning with the updater disabled.
quote: Compared with the original Qwen3-1.7B model, the Sudoku-trained adapter improves zero-shot accuracy from 72.36% to 72.96% on MATH-Hard and from 50.75% to 55.38% on CruxEval-O.

title: Implementasi Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) Pada Kasus Klasifikasi
claim: Simulated HRM performs well on 30-feature data but overfits or collapses on low-dimensional data.
quote: Sebaliknya, pada dataset Diabetes (8 fitur), model mengalami overfitting ekstrem dengan akurasi 71%, sementara pada dataset Iris (4 fitur), model mengalami mode collapse dengan akurasi hanya 33,3%.

title: How Much Is One Recurrence Worth? Iso-Depth Scaling Laws for Looped Language Models
claim: At matched training compute and matched effective depth, replacing unique blocks with shared recurrences raises validation loss; one recurrence is worth r^0.46 in unique-parameter terms.
quote: Our φ = 0.46 sits in between, so replacing unique blocks with shared recurrences increases validation loss at matched training compute.

title: How Much Is One Recurrence Worth? Iso-Depth Scaling Laws for Looped Language Models
claim: The compute-optimal loss gap of looped vs non-looped grows with r and persists at ~20x the grid compute (0.061 nats at r=4, 47B tokens).
quote: The looped model trails by 0.061 nats in validation loss, inside the [0.05, 0.08] nats r=4 band measured across the grid.

title: How Much Is One Recurrence Worth? Iso-Depth Scaling Laws for Looped Language Models
claim: Truncated BPTT (backprop through last ceil(r/2) loops) lowers validation loss via more tokens but lowers phi to 0.38, i.e. the loop mechanism is trained worse and the optimum shifts to wider, costlier models.
quote: However, the measured φ disagrees, dropping from 0.45 to 0.38 (Table 3). So each additional recurrence is now worth much less in unique-parameter terms than before

title: How Much Is One Recurrence Worth? Iso-Depth Scaling Laws for Looped Language Models
claim: Hyperconnections at the loop boundary raise phi to 0.65 and move the compute optimum to narrower widths (a genuine capacity gain); r=2 matches or beats r=1 at some budgets.
quote: hyperconnections substantially lower validation loss across all looped runs, and φ jumps from 0.45 to 0.65 (Table 3).

title: How Much Is One Recurrence Worth? Iso-Depth Scaling Laws for Looped Language Models
claim: Downstream, parametric-knowledge tasks track the looped models' capacity loss while reasoning-heavy axes show no above-noise looped advantage, even at the extrapolation run.
quote: Parametric-knowledge tasks track validation loss directly, while reasoning-heavy tasks on which looped models are predicted to excel show no above-noise architectural signal at our budgets, not even at the ∼20× extrapolation runs.

title: How Much Is One Recurrence Worth? Iso-Depth Scaling Laws for Looped Language Models
claim: Literature synthesis: in trained looped LMs effective inference depth concentrates near the training depth distribution rather than extrapolating past it, so r is treated as an architectural rather than test-time axis.
quote: Taken together, effective inference depth in trained looped LMs concentrates near the training depth distribution rather than extrapolating freely past it.

title: Scaling Laws for Looped Mixture of Experts
claim: Recurrence adds effective parameters only up to a finite asymptote; MoE sparsity raises that asymptote and delays saturation (routing reaches different experts across passes).
quote: Finding: Scaling recurrence adds effective-parameter gain up to a finite, sparsity-dependent asymptote, while scaling sparsity raises and sustains this gain over more recurrent passes.

title: Scaling Laws for Looped Mixture of Experts
claim: The bounded mapping extrapolates better to unseen R=16 than linear (overestimates) and power-law (overly optimistic) mappings used by prior looped scaling laws.
quote: The linear mapping substantially overestimates the effective-parameter gain, while the power-law mapping captures diminishing gains but remains overly optimistic beyond the fitted range.

title: Scaling Laws for Looped Mixture of Experts
claim: At matched training FLOPs (E=8), more recurrence lets a smaller model match a model with about 2x the total parameters on reasoning (GSM8K, BBH).
quote: These recurrence gains can offset a ∼2× increase in total parameters on Reasoning: at 1021 FLOPs, the 0.3B model with R≥4 matches or exceeds the 0.6B model with R=1, while the 0.6B model with R≥3 matches the 1.0B model with R=1.

title: Scaling Laws for Looped Mixture of Experts
claim: At trillion-token scale and matched training compute, a 1.3B-total looped MoE with law-derived recurrence matches a 2.9B-total non-looped MoE on reasoning but trails on the 14-benchmark overall score, and uses more inference compute.
quote: Despite using ∼2× fewer active and total parameters, A0.3B-1.3B LoopMoE at R ∈ {4, 5} matches A0.6B-2.9B MoE on reasoning tasks (BBH, GSM8K) by using more inference compute, while trailing on Overall performance.

title: Scaling Laws for Looped Mixture of Experts
claim: Compute-optimal recurrence grows with training budget and sparsity; under fixed compute, tight weight-memory budgets favor recurrence and large budgets favor sparsity.
quote: Finding: At fixed compute, tight memory favors recurrence, and more memory favors sparsity.

title: SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers
claim: With per-token FLOPs, total parameters and KV cache matched, the looped MoE (SMELT) reaches lower loss than the unlooped MoE at every scale and sparsity level.
quote: SMELT reaches lower loss than the Baseline at every scale and sparsity level.

title: SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers
claim: On the fitted compute-optimal frontier SMELT saves 6.8-10.0% of training compute at 1e20 FLOPs and 14.7-18.0% at 1e21 FLOPs, with the saving growing with compute because its frontier exponent is larger.
quote: At C = 1020 , SMELT saves 6.8–10.0% of training compute across sparsity levels. At C = 1021 , the range widens to 14.7–18.0%.

title: SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers
claim: Downstream gains exceed what the validation-loss gap predicts, and this excess grows with scale; at 1.6B the largest excess shifts to Symbolic Problem Solving.
quote: SMELT wins on DCLM Completion in 96 of 96 matched pairs, on DCLM Core in 83 of 96, and on MMLU in 29 of the 30 pairs whose Baseline scores at least 10 percentage points above chance

title: SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers
claim: Under matched FLOPs, looping twice beats three or four loops because extra visits force a thinner model; looping the middle half beats full-stack looping.
quote: Two visits win on all three metrics (Table 5); both a third and a fourth visit regress because the matched FLOPs cap forces a thinner model.

title: SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers
claim: The looping gain is largest on Code and structured data, concentrates on long samples, and grows when in-context examples are provided.
quote: CE Gain is positive on all five categories. Code leads at 20.4%; Finance and Math/STEM follow at 16.8% and 16.6%; Knowledge and Web sit at 14.9% and 14.8%.

title: Parcae: Scaling Laws For Stable Looped Language Models
claim: Instability of prior looped models (residual explosion) is tied to learning an injection transition with spectral radius >= 1; constraining it yields convergence across learning rates where baselines diverge.
quote: Figure 3 and Table 2 confirm this empirically: divergent runs learn a spectral radius of ρ(A) ≥ 1, with convergent runs maintaining ρ(A) < 1, affirming that LTI stability constraints are necessary.

title: Parcae: Scaling Laws For Stable Looped Language Models
claim: At matched unique parameters and training tokens (but more FLOPs for Parcae, mu_rec=8 on the middle third), Parcae beats Transformers on validation PPL and Core/Core-Extended at all four scales up to 1.3B.
quote: Table 5 shows that Parcae reduces validation perplexity by 4.3–9.2% and improves Core and Core-Extended Scores by up to 2.99 and 1.18 points, respectively.

title: Parcae: Scaling Laws For Stable Looped Language Models
claim: At fixed parameter count and fixed training FLOPs, the compute-optimal looped frontier (fewer tokens, more recurrence) achieves strictly lower loss and higher Core than fixed-depth models that spend the FLOPs on more data.
quote: Figure 6 shows fixed-depth Parcae models without looping at each FLOP budget. The optimal curve achieves a strictly lower loss, which translates to 1.2-2.0 points higher Core scores (Table 6).

title: Parcae: Scaling Laws For Stable Looped Language Models
claim: Compute-optimal training increases mean recurrence and data in tandem following power laws.
quote: Our initial scaling laws suggest that looping and data should be increased in tandem, given a fixed FLOP budget.

title: Parcae: Scaling Laws For Stable Looped Language Models
claim: Test-time looping does not extrapolate past training depth in language modeling: gains plateau near the training mean recurrence and follow a saturating exponential.
quote: we observe that gains plateau near µrec , suggesting training depth determines the test-time scaling ceiling.

title: Parcae: Scaling Laws For Stable Looped Language Models
claim: Truncating the sampling distribution by the backprop depth hurts extrapolation to lower and higher recurrences, and deeper test-time recurrence quality is coupled to the backprop depth.
quote: This implies that the capabilities of looped models utilizing deeper recurrences are heavily coupled with µbwd .

title: Nanbeige4.2-3B: Unlocking Agentic Capabilities in a Compact Model
claim: With 3B non-embedding parameters the post-trained looped model beats larger public models (Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma4-12B) on all reported general-agent and code-agent benchmarks; comparison is against checkpoints trained on different data and recipes.
quote: With only 3B non-embedding parameters, Nanbeige4.2-3B achieves the best results on all reported general-agent and code-agent benchmarks, outperforming the larger Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma4-12B models.

title: Nanbeige4.2-3B: Unlocking Agentic Capabilities in a Compact Model
claim: Training the looped architecture from scratch performs significantly better than upcycling a pretrained standard Transformer into a looped one (no numbers reported).
quote: In our experiments, the from-scratch approach performs significantly better, suggesting that the model benefits from adapting representations to repeated layer reuse throughout pre-training

title: Nanbeige4.2-3B: Unlocking Agentic Capabilities in a Compact Model
claim: Two passes give the best trade-off, retaining about 75% of a standard Transformer's token efficiency; more passes add little, slow training and destabilize optimization.
quote: A two-pass configuration provides the most favorable trade-off in our experiments: relative to a standard Transformer, it retains approximately 75% of the token efficiency and provides a significant capacity gain.

title: Nanbeige4.2-3B: Unlocking Agentic Capabilities in a Compact Model
claim: Sharing the KV cache across loop passes halves KV memory but consistently yields lower gains than the full non-sharing loop, so it was not used.
quote: Although the sharing configuration reduces the KV-cache by half, its performance gains are consistently lower than those of the full, non-sharing loop configuration.

title: Nanbeige4.2-3B: Unlocking Agentic Capabilities in a Compact Model
claim: The looped base model improves on the non-looped predecessor Nanbeige4-3B-Base and beats similar-size public base models, but the gain conflates the loop with a new 28T-token data recipe.
quote: The results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining the Looped Transformer structure with the improved pre-training data recipe.

title: LoopCoder-v2: Only Loop Once for Efficient Test-Time Computation Scaling
claim: With identical parameters, 18T-token pretraining data and SFT, the two-loop PLT improves broadly over the non-looped baseline on code generation, code reasoning, agentic SWE and tool use.
quote: the two-loop variant delivers broad gains over the non-looped baseline across code generation, code reasoning, agentic software engineering, and tool-use benchmarks, improving SWEbench Verified from 43.0 to 64.4 points and Multi-SWE from 14.0 to 31.0 points.

title: LoopCoder-v2: Only Loop Once for Efficient Test-Time Computation Scaling
claim: Loop count is strongly non-monotonic: three or more loops regress, often below the non-looped baseline (R=3 drops to 27.6% on SWE-bench Verified).
quote: the two-loop model improves broadly over the non-looped baseline, including a gain on SWE-bench Verified from 43.0% to 64.4%, while the three-loop model regresses on many tasks, dropping to 27.6% on SWE-bench Verified.

title: LoopCoder-v2: Only Loop Once for Efficient Test-Time Computation Scaling
claim: Per-loop diagnostics: loop 2 is the main site of refinement; beyond it updates become oscillatory and representational diversity shrinks while the cross-loop-offset cost stays fixed and dominates.
quote: At every extra loop the offset cost exceeds the per-loop gain by 30–45×, so the fixed offset tax dominates the shrinking refinement beyond loop 2.

title: LoopCoder-v2: Only Loop Once for Efficient Test-Time Computation Scaling
claim: Explicit CoT (thinking SFT) and latent looping are complementary and super-additive on reasoning-heavy tasks at R=2.
quote: Table 4 shows that on reasoning-heavy tasks the thinking variant improves over the instructiontuned variant by a wide margin, most strikingly on LiveCodeBench (+26.9 points)

title: LoopCoder-v2: Only Loop Once for Efficient Test-Time Computation Scaling
claim: The 7B R=2 model is competitive with much larger open models on SWE-bench Verified (cross-model comparison with different data).
quote: this single extra loop makes our 7B model strikingly competitive with far larger systems, most notably on SWE-bench Verified, where it reaches 64.4%, surpassing 30B–72B open models

title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models
claim: Ouro 1.4B and 2.6B (4 loops, 7.7T tokens) match 4B and 8B public dense transformers on most benchmarks, i.e. 2-3x parameter efficiency; baselines trained on different data (2T-36T tokens).
quote: we demonstrate that 1.4B and 2.6B parameter LoopLMs match 4B and 8B standard transformers on most benchmarks, yielding 2-3× parameter-efficiency gains

title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models
claim: Looping does not increase knowledge storage: looped and non-looped models of equal parameter count store about 2 bits per parameter on Capo synthetic biographies.
quote: looping does not increase knowledge capacity nor improve capacity scaling. Models with and without loops all attain around a similar capacity ratio ≈ 2 bits/parameter.

title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models
claim: On the Mano modular-arithmetic manipulation task, looped models beat iso-parameter non-looped models for all k and often beat the iso-FLOP (12-layer, iso-effective-depth) baseline.
quote: given the same parameters, looped models always outperform their non-looped counterpart for all possible k ∈ {2, 3, 6}. Even with the same number of FLOPs in the model, the looped models can often perform better.

title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models
claim: Test-time depth extrapolation beyond the trained 4 steps degrades benchmark accuracy for both base and Thinking models, although HEx-PHI safety keeps improving at steps 5-8.
quote: benchmark performance sees a moderate degradation when extrapolating, with a noticeable drop compared to the peak at T = 4.

title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models
claim: In the small-scale controlled sweep (20B tokens), a standard transformer whose layer count is multiplied by the recurrent step always beats the LoopLM; the gap grows with loops and shrinks with model size.
quote: Overall, the performance of the standard model exceeds that of LoopLM under the same conditions. This gap increases with the recurrent step and decreases with the model size.

title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models
claim: Gains from loop 1 to loop 4 on MMLU concentrate on reasoning-heavy subcategories and are smallest on fact-retrieval subcategories.
quote: The categories with the most significant improvements are those requiring logical, maths, or procedural reasoning; conversely, categories that depend more on retrieving specific, memorized facts or nuanced world knowledge showed the most modest gains.

title: Sparse Layers are Critical to Scaling Looped Language Models
claim: At matched training compute and effective depth, dense looping scales strictly worse than the dense baseline, while Looped-MoE scales better than the dense baseline.
quote: We find that Looped-MoE scales better than Base, while Looped models scale strictly worse (Figure 1, middle), supporting our hypothesis that sparse routing restores expressiveness lost to weight tying.

title: Sparse Layers are Critical to Scaling Looped Language Models
claim: Looping the same architecture always reduces quality at matched compute: non-looped MoE beats Looped-MoE and Base beats Looped; all four share roughly the same slope and differ in offset.
quote: MoE scales the best, followed by Looped-MoE, then Base and lastly Looped. Looping the same architecture seems thus to strictly reduce expressivity.

title: Sparse Layers are Critical to Scaling Looped Language Models
claim: Downstream at 1e18 FLOPs, Looped-MoE has the highest OLMES Core 9 average with fewer stored parameters than Base; dense Looped is lowest; non-looped MoE is lowest overall despite best test loss.
quote: Looped-MoE achieves the highest average score (39.6) across the Core 9 benchmarks, outperforming Base (38.7) despite storing fewer unique parameters (216M vs. 246M). Looped scores lowest (37.4)

title: Sparse Layers are Critical to Scaling Looped Language Models
claim: MoE routing diverges across loop passes, so the same physical layer runs different expert sub-networks on each pass.
quote: Across layers 1–6 and 8, 25–53% of tokens receive entirely non-overlapping expert assignments between passes, while only 4–14% receive identical assignments.

title: Sparse Layers are Critical to Scaling Looped Language Models
claim: Looped models give better training-free early-exit compute-quality trade-offs than non-looped models, and more loops improve this further.
quote: at 10% FLOPs saved, Looped and Looped-MoE reach perplexity 50.2 and 51.0, compared to 55.4 for Base and 75.7 for MoE.

title: Sparse Layers are Critical to Scaling Looped Language Models
claim: Critique of Ouro: Ouro compares by unique parameters while giving its models 4x the effective depth (more compute) than the dense models it is compared to.
quote: In their study, they compare performance by the number of unique parameters, but giving their models much more compute (4x the effective depth) than the models in their comparisons.

title: Looped Language Models Improve Compositional Tool Calling
claim: Under matched SFT, looped models do better on compositional (multi-call, nested) tool calling, while gains on isolated single API calls are smaller and model-dependent; the Ouro comparison is against non-looped models with different pretraining.
quote: In both experimental settings, looped models perform better on compositional tool-calling tasks, whereas gains on isolated API invocation are smaller and model-dependent.

title: Looped Language Models Improve Compositional Tool Calling
claim: Holding the fine-tuned model fixed and only varying inference depth, BFCL accuracy rises with recurrent depth, mostly on compositional categories, before plateauing.
quote: Figure 2 shows that BFCL accuracy generally rises with recurrent depth, with the largest gains on compositional categories.

title: Looped Language Models Improve Compositional Tool Calling
claim: Adaptive exit with Ouro's gate recovers most of the deep-recurrence gain with fewer iterations per token, matching or slightly exceeding the best fixed depth on BFCL.
quote: On BFCL, adaptive stopping matches or slightly exceeds the best fixed-depth operating point while executing fewer recurrent iterations on average.

title: Looped Language Models Improve Compositional Tool Calling
claim: Retrofitted looped models improve several compositional categories over their parents but remain much weaker than natively pretrained looped models on deeply nested workflows.
quote: although post-hoc recurrence improves several compositional tasks, retrofitted models remain substantially weaker than natively recurrent models on deeply nested workflows

title: Squeezing More from Limited Data with Recursive Transformers
claim: At a fixed 10M-word data budget, a 27.6M recursive model beats both the best standard model and an unfactorized standard model on all three evaluations (same data, fewer params, more FLOPs).
quote: Overall, the recursive models are highly competitive; in the 10M-word setting, our recursive model outperforms both standard models on all three evaluations.

title: Squeezing More from Limited Data with Recursive Transformers
claim: At 100M words, the 404M RecursiveGPT-Large reaches the best average score, above a 1.22B standard model trained on the same data, while the 124M recursive model trails the 1.22B model except on BLiMP.
quote: Scaling the recursive model to 404.1M parameters yields RecursiveGPT-Large, which uses substantially higher compute and reaches the best average score among our models while still being smaller than the 1.22B standard baseline.

title: Squeezing More from Limited Data with Recursive Transformers
claim: Allocating the recursive model's extra compute to more epochs over the same data instead degrades the standard model, so recursion is a better use of FLOPs when data is the binding constraint.
quote: Additional epochs reduce the average score from 45.07 to 41.47 at 10M words and from 63.47 to 56.68 at 100M words.

title: Squeezing More from Limited Data with Recursive Transformers
claim: The benefit of recurrent depth is non-monotonic: average score improves up to depth 16 and then declines slightly, attributed to optimization difficulty.
quote: the average score across the three evaluations improves with recurrent depth up to depth 16 and then declines slightly.

title: Beyond What Seems Necessary: Hidden Gains from Scaling Training-Time Reasoning Length under Outcome Supervision
claim: With parameters and data fixed, increasing training-time loop count keeps improving OOD accuracy long after ID accuracy saturates.
quote: Increasing the loop count yields OOD gains up to around 44 loops, while ID accuracy saturates near 100% by around 2 loops.

title: Beyond What Seems Necessary: Hidden Gains from Scaling Training-Time Reasoning Length under Outcome Supervision
claim: The OOD gains from more loops persist when explicit loop-index embeddings are added, peaking around 36 loops.
quote: ID accuracy saturates around 2 loops, while OOD accuracy continues improving up to around 36 loops.

title: Beyond What Seems Necessary: Hidden Gains from Scaling Training-Time Reasoning Length under Outcome Supervision
claim: Under outcome-only supervision, OOD robustness may require a larger reasoning-length budget than ID validation alone indicates.
quote: This suggests that robustness may require a larger budget than ID validation alone would indicate.

title: Evaluating Tiny Recursive Models Across Training for Code Generation
claim: At equal parameters, TRM-AR fits, generates and generalizes better than a 2-layer Transformer, recovering roughly half of the gap to the 20-layer control.
quote: At equal parameters, TRM-AR fits, generates, and generalizes better than the parameter-matched control while recovering approximately 45% of the validation-loss gap and 57% of the generation-quality gap between the two controls

title: Evaluating Tiny Recursive Models Across Training for Code Generation
claim: At equal effective depth, a 20-layer Transformer with ~10x the non-embedding parameters fits and generates better at its validation optimum; TRM-AR's remaining advantage is resistance to overfitting.
quote: However, at equal effective depth, the larger transformer fits and generates better at its validation optimum, suggesting TRM-AR’s advantage lies in resistance to overfitting, not greater capability.

title: Evaluating Tiny Recursive Models Across Training for Code Generation
claim: Recursion is parameter-efficient but not compute-efficient: per-step time is ~175x the iso-parameter control and ~2.4x the iso-depth control.
quote: Realizing an effective depth of 20 by looping a two-layer block costs roughly 175× the per-step time of the iso-parameter control and about 2.4× that of the iso-depth control

title: LatentMT: Machine Translation with Latent Reasoning
claim: LatentMT with a 2.6B looped backbone is comparable to models three to five times larger across 32 translation directions; comparisons are against models with different pretraining.
quote: Across 32 translation directions spanning high-, mid-, and low-resource languages, LatentMT achieves performance comparable to models three to five times larger.

title: LatentMT: Machine Translation with Latent Reasoning
claim: Translation quality improves with recurrent steps early and then saturates; most of the gain is from u=1 to u=2.
quote: Most of the gain from additional recurrent computation appears early: moving from u = 1 to u = 2 adds 7.65 BLEU, 9.35 COMET, and 9.86 COMETKiwi

title: LatentMT: Machine Translation with Latent Reasoning
claim: Under an identical fine-tuning protocol, the best LatentMT checkpoint beats Qwen3-8B SFT on all three DRT metrics and by 5.31 BLEU on ArzEn-MultiGenre (pretraining differs).
quote: LatentMT achieves the best overall score among all compared systems, peaking at 24.47 BLEU with u = 4. This is 7.28 BLEU above fine-tuned Google NMT and 5.31 BLEU above Qwen3-8B SFT

title: How Model Growth, Recursion, and Boundary Operators Influence Scaling Exponents
claim: Architectural changes can alter the compute-optimal scaling exponent: model growth gives the largest gain and a boundary operator alone also raises it, with compute multipliers over Vanilla that grow with scale.
quote: Growing the model during training, by increasing the number of core passes with untied weights, improves the scaling exponent. The grown model reaches the loss of a standard transformer with 1.55× less compute at 1020 FLOPs, and this gap widens with scale.

title: How Model Growth, Recursion, and Boundary Operators Influence Scaling Exponents
claim: At matched FLOPs and executed depth, weight tying (Loop-2) versus untied cores (Untied-2) costs a fixed compute factor that does not grow with scale.
quote: Weight sharing therefore costs a fixed factor of compute at every scale, rather than a factor that grows with the budget.

title: How Model Growth, Recursion, and Boundary Operators Influence Scaling Exponents
claim: Growing the number of tied loops during training keeps Vanilla's parameter count yet gives a 1.36x compute multiplier over a standard transformer at 1e20 FLOPs.
quote: Growing the number of loops with tied weights obtains the exponent improvement from growth with the same number of parameters as a vanilla transformer, and trails untied growth by only a small constant factor, for a 1.36× compute multiplier over a standard transformer at 1020 FLOPs.

title: How Model Growth, Recursion, and Boundary Operators Influence Scaling Exponents
claim: With repeated data, looping regularizes: the optimal loop count grows with compute and loop scaling beats weight-decay-tuned model-size scaling by 2.2x compute; untied looping does not beat tuned Operator-1.
quote: Scaling the loop count at fixed model size and fixed weight decay matches that loss with 2.2× less compute, and tuning weight decay on top gains at most 0.02, so loop-count scaling is more compute-efficient and nearly free of tuning.

title: How Model Growth, Recursion, and Boundary Operators Influence Scaling Exponents
claim: A 7.4B Untied-Grow model matches the estimated GPT-3 13B CORE score with about 20x less compute; the authors flag this as indicative only (different data and evaluation).
quote: The two models were trained on different data, and the GPT-3 reference is an estimate from a separate evaluation pipeline, so the roughly 20× gap is indicative rather than a controlled comparison.

title: Beyond Parameters: Exploring Virtual Logic Depth for Scaling Laws
claim: At fixed parameters, adding virtual depth through layer reuse leaves knowledge capacity nearly unchanged, while capacity scales with parameter count across models.
quote: At a fixed parameter count, VLD leaves knowledge capacity nearly unchanged (with only minor variance), while across models knowledge capacity scales with the number of parameters

title: Beyond Parameters: Exploring Virtual Logic Depth for Scaling Laws
claim: Layer reuse substantially improves synthetic multi-step math reasoning at fixed parameters.
quote: the cycle pattern achieves substantial improvements, increasing the 4-layer model’s accuracy from 46.3% to 70.7% with a VLD factor of 5.

title: Beyond Parameters: Exploring Virtual Logic Depth for Scaling Laws
claim: At equal effective depth (12), a 50M looped model slightly exceeds a native 150M 12-layer model on iGSM op15.
quote: For instance, the 50M-parameter model using the cycle pattern (factor 2, effective depth=12) achieves 62.05% accuracy, surpassing the native 150Mparameter model (12-layer)

title: Beyond Parameters: Exploring Virtual Logic Depth for Scaling Laws
claim: Scaling with VLD is non-monotonic in places (factor 3 below factor 2; depth 32 below depth 16).
quote: cycle pattern shows VLD factor 3 (61.6%) performing slightly worse than factor 2 (62.1%) for the 4-layer model, and Figure 3(c) shows depth 32 yielding lower accuracy than depth 16.

title: Scaling Laws vs Model Architectures: How does Inductive Bias Influence Scaling?
claim: Universal Transformers are among the architectures that are difficult to scale, especially downstream, compared with the vanilla Transformer.
quote: there are models which are difficult to scale such as LConv, UT, MLP-Mixer and Performer. This is even more evident on downstream task.

title: Scaling Laws vs Model Architectures: How does Inductive Bias Influence Scaling?
claim: Increasing the number of UT recurrent operations did not improve performance even though it increased FLOPs.
quote: Initially we tried scaling the number of recurrent operations. However, we found that even with an increase of FLOPS, this does not lead to improved performance.

title: Scaling Laws vs Model Architectures: How does Inductive Bias Influence Scaling?
claim: Seq2seq ALBERT (parameters shared across all layers and encoder/decoder) scales negatively as model size grows.
quote: We also note that ALBERT scales (trends) negatively2 (gets worse) as we scale the model up.

title: Looped GPT-BERT: Trading Parameters for Computation in Small Language Modeling
claim: With far fewer parameters, the looped model is comparable to public BabyLM Strict-small baselines on selected linguistic and downstream metrics (baselines differ in size and recipe).
quote: Compared with public BabyLM 10M Strict-small GPT-2 and GPT-BERT baselines, it achieves comparable performance on selected linguistic and downstream metrics, including BLiMP and GLUE, with fewer parameters.

title: Looped GPT-BERT: Trading Parameters for Computation in Small Language Modeling
claim: More loops help training and preserve linguistic performance, but weaker results on other tasks suggest few physical layers restrict representational space.
quote: whereas poorer performance on other tasks may reveal an inherent limitation of the looped design: using only a few physical layers restricts the model's representational space.

title: Self-Attentive Model for Headline Generation
claim: A Universal Transformer achieves state-of-the-art headline generation on NYT versus prior published systems.
quote: we applied recent Universal Transformer architecture paired with byte-pair encoding technique and achieved new state-of-the-art results on the New York Times Annotated corpus with ROUGE-L F1-score 24.84 and ROUGE-2 F1-score 13.48.

title: Visual Implicit Autoregressive Modeling
claim: With 38% of VAR-d30's parameters, VIAR reaches FID 2.16 vs VAR's 2.08 at CFG 1.5 (slightly worse FID, better sFID).
quote: In particular, VIAR achieves about 2.16 FID with 770.9M parameters, closely tracking a 2.0B-parameter explicit model at 2.08 FID.

title: Visual Implicit Autoregressive Modeling
claim: VIAR uses fewer inference FLOPs than VAR-d30 at every schedule and can trade quality for compute within one trained model.
quote: As shown in the Table 5, VAR requires 1.88 TFLOPs, while VIAR ranges from 0.84 TFLOPs to 1.46 TFLOPs depending on the selected schedule.

title: Visual Implicit Autoregressive Modeling
claim: Fixed-point iterations converge rapidly (cosine similarity about 0.985 by iteration 5), so high-resolution scales need few iterations.
quote: achieves 0.985 by iteration 5 and approaches 0.999 by iteration 10, indicating that the fixed-point iteration converges rapidly.

title: Visual Implicit Autoregressive Modeling
claim: Training memory stays essentially constant with explicit depth for VIAR, while VAR's grows linearly.
quote: VAR's memory grows roughly linearly with depth, whereas VIAR stays essentially constant because the implicit equilibrium architecture.

title: Self-composing neural operators for high-frequency and multiscale PDE surrogates
claim: Tied self-composed operators reach accuracy competitive with their untied counterparts at a fraction of the parameters on Darcy benchmarks.
quote: MgNOself achieves competitive accuracy with only 0.17M parameters compared to 0.57M for MgNO, while FNO2D-self uses 0.56M versus 2.37M for FNO2D.

title: Self-composing neural operators for high-frequency and multiscale PDE surrogates
claim: Weight tying does not reduce activation memory or wall-clock training at matched unroll depth; the gain is parameter efficiency and regularization.
quote: It is worth noting, however, that lower parameter count does not by itself imply lower activation memory or shorter wall-clock training time.

title: Self-composing neural operators for high-frequency and multiscale PDE surrogates
claim: In a controlled 400 kHz ablation, self-composition helps only the multigrid backbone; regular FNO and UNet are slightly better than their self-composed versions.
quote: For FNO and UNet, the regular and self-composed variants remain close, with the regular models slightly better in this short run (0.0902 versus 0.0966 for FNO and 0.2559 versus 0.2610 for UNet).

title: Self-composing neural operators for high-frequency and multiscale PDE surrogates
claim: Train-and-Unroll reaches lower loss than direct training at the target depth; training error decays nearly geometrically with depth then saturates above machine precision.
quote: T&U reaches lower loss than direct target-depth training while still providing usable intermediate models O(3) and O(4) before the final O(5)

title: Learning to Stop Overthinking at Test Time
claim: A recurrent model with 24 iterations outperforms a feed-forward network of equivalent computational depth, and harder corruption levels need more iterations to reach the same accuracy.
quote: Notably, a recurrent model with 24 iterations outperforms a feed-forward network with equivalent computational depth, emphasizing the effectiveness of dynamic depth adjustment.

title: Learning to Stop Overthinking at Test Time
claim: Recurrent models use about one-sixth the parameters of feed-forward networks while generalizing better to corruptions.
quote: Recurrent models also demonstrate remarkable parameter efficiency, as shown in Table 1, using only one-sixth the parameters of feed-forward networks while achieving superior generalization.

title: Learning to Stop Overthinking at Test Time
claim: Halting-as-early-as-possible heuristics (ACT) limit extrapolation; selecting the iteration by self-supervised accuracy performs better.
quote: We show that the early stopping heuristic in previous works—which forces the model to halt as soon as possible—limits the extrapolation capabilities of RNNs.

title: FlexiGPT: Pruning and Extending Large Language Models with Low-Rank Weight Sharing
claim: At the same 30% compression of Llama-2 7B, weight-shared replacement blocks beat block pruning baselines (ShortGPT, ShortGPT+LoRA) on most benchmarks.
quote: Our method, FlexiGPT, shows the lowest PPL of 6.55 at a 30% pruning ratio, outperforming both ShortGPT and ShortGPT + LoRA.

title: FlexiGPT: Pruning and Extending Large Language Models with Low-Rank Weight Sharing
claim: Repeating TinyLlama blocks with unique LoRA (22 to 36 effective layers) slightly improves PPL and zero-shot accuracy at the same continued-pretraining budget, but costs about 39% more compute time.
quote: FlexiGPT (Block) achieves the lowest PPL of 6.73, compared to the base model's 6.84, indicating a more efficient model.

title: FlexiGPT: Pruning and Extending Large Language Models with Low-Rank Weight Sharing
claim: Weight-shared replacement keeps the dense model's compute cost: it reduces stored parameters but not inference time, unlike block-dropping.
quote: Although our method is slower than ShortGPT, this is expected, as our approach involves replacing the pruned blocks with weightsharing techniques.

title: Merging Feed-Forward Sublayers for Compressed Transformers
claim: Removing a third of FFN sublayers by merging leaves performance almost unchanged across vision, LM and MT.
quote: identical to the original model, resulting in only a 1% accuracy drop in ViT, 1 PPL increase in GPT-2, and 2 BLEU drop in the translation model.

title: Merging Feed-Forward Sublayers for Compressed Transformers
claim: Merging consistently matches or outperforms dropping layers at approximately matched parameter reduction.
quote: As seen in the figure, our method consistently matches or outperforms the layer-dropping method.

title: Transformer Layers as Painters
claim: Replacing a span of middle layers with copies of the center layer (training-free looping of one layer) is catastrophic and worse than skipping those layers.
quote: No, sharing weights among middle layers is catastrophic, indicating that the middle layers are performing different functions.

title: Transformer Layers as Painters
claim: Looping the averaged parallel middle block three times significantly improves over a single parallel pass, and is the least harmful variant overall.
quote: In Figure 9, we show the results for looping the parallelized layer 3 times. As can be seen in Figure 11, this method (Looped Parallel 3X) significantly improves on a single iteration (Parallel Layer).

title: Transformer Layers as Painters
claim: The best number of loop iterations grows roughly linearly with the number of parallelized layers.
quote: Yes, with the optimal number of iterations proportional to the number of parallelized layers.

title: Transformer Layers as Painters
claim: Math and reasoning tasks are more sensitive to layer order than semantic tasks.
quote: Yes! Mathematical and reasoning tasks are more order dependent than "semantic" tasks.

title: Transformers Learn to Implement Multi-step Gradient Descent with Chain of Thought
claim: With loops L = Omega(log d), the looped linear transformer's global minimizer reaches arbitrarily small polynomial loss and is strictly better than the non-looped one-layer transformer for L >= 2.
quote: Moreover, the asymptotic loss is strictly better than that of the non-looped one-layer transformer when L ≥ 2, thus establishing the separation between looped and non-looped transformers.

title: Transformers Learn to Implement Multi-step Gradient Descent with Chain of Thought
claim: Gatmiry et al.'s earlier bound for looped transformers implementing multi-step GD was no better than a single GD step; this paper closes that gap.
quote: Notably, the looped transformer in [20] that implements multi-step gradient descent is shown to be no better than the transformer performing a single gradient descent step.

title: Transformers Learn to Implement Multi-step Gradient Descent with Chain of Thought
claim: CoT and looping are two routes to the same iterative algorithm: both can naturally implement gradient descent.
quote: The key connection between our work and Gatmiry et al. [20] lies in the observation that both looped transformers and transformers with CoT prompting through autoregressive generation are capable of naturally implementing iterative algorithms like gradient descent.

title: TroL: Traversal of Layers for Large Language and Vision Models
claim: Turning on layer traversing improves TroL-1.8B on MMStar from 36.0 to 45.5 and MM-Vet from 34.6 to 45.1 at essentially the same parameters and data.

title: TroL: Traversal of Layers for Large Language and Vision Models
claim: Layer traversing also improves other LLVMs (DeepSeek-VL-1.3B, MiniCPM-V2-2.8B, LLaVA-NeXT-7B) trained on the same instruction data.
quote: In Table 6, we have applied layer traversing to other LLVMs such as DeepSeek-VL-1.3B, MiniCPMV2-2.8B, and LLaVA-NeXT-7B. This adjustment aims to validate the effectiveness of layer traversing under a fairer comparison setting

title: TroL: Traversal of Layers for Large Language and Vision Models
claim: Traversal mostly happens in shallow layers; deeper layers barely use it.
quote: the layer traversing event of looking back and retracing the answering stream mostly occurs in shallower layers, while the deeper layers are not involved in traversing.

title: TroL: Traversal of Layers for Large Language and Vision Models
claim: TroL outperforms larger open-source LLVMs on reported benchmarks (cross-model comparison).
quote: TroL employs a simple layer traversing approach yet efficiently outperforms the open-source LLVMs with larger model sizes and rivals the performances of the closed-source LLVMs with substantial sizes.

title: NeuralSolver: Learning Algorithms For Consistent and Efficient Extrapolation Across General Tasks
claim: NeuralSolver reaches 100% on Prefix-Sum and Maze when evaluated on inputs 16x and 5x larger than training, and 84.30% average on Chess.
quote: our approach is able to achieve a 100% accuracy on the Prefix-Sum and Maze tasks, when evaluated on a scenario with observations 16 and 5 times bigger, respectively, than during training.

title: NeuralSolver: Learning Algorithms For Consistent and Efficient Extrapolation Across General Tasks
claim: Uses 92% fewer parameters than DT-Recall on different-size tasks and less than 30% of its MACs per training example.
quote: NeuralSolver employs the same architecture across all different-size tasks, with 0.23 million total parameters. This corresponds to a 92% reduction in the number of parameters

title: NeuralSolver: Learning Algorithms For Consistent and Efficient Extrapolation Across General Tasks
claim: A gated (LSTM) recurrent block extrapolates much better than a recurrent ResNet block, and curriculum training helps on some tasks.
quote: The use of an LSTM layer instead of a ResNet block in the recurrent convolutional module results in a significant improvement in performance.

title: Adaptive recurrent vision performs zero-shot computation scaling to unseen difficulty levels
claim: AdRNNs zero-shot generalize to harder unseen difficulty levels by increasing recurrent iterations at test time.
quote: these RNNs zero-shot generalize to more difficult problem settings not shown during training by dynamically increasing the number of recurrent iterations at test time.

title: Adaptive recurrent vision performs zero-shot computation scaling to unseen difficulty levels
claim: A plain weight-tied residual network (R-ResNet-30) without gating could not learn PathFinder or Mazes in this setup.
quote: The simpler recurrent network without gating, weight-tied R-ResNet-30, was unable to learn on PathFinder and on Mazes highlighting the importance of specialized operations such as gating and backpropagation through time.

title: Adaptive recurrent vision performs zero-shot computation scaling to unseen difficulty levels
claim: Learned ACT halting outperforms halting based on hidden-state stability; stability halting fails entirely on PathFinder-21/24.
quote: AdRNNs perform better than hConvGRU (stable halting) on both datasets; especially, stable halting completely fails to show generalization to PathFinder-21 and -24.

title: Iterative convergent computation may not be a useful inductive bias for residual neural networks
claim: Conventionally trained ResNets can express but do not learn iterative solutions.
quote: Consistent with previous work, we show that, even though ResNets can express iterative solutions, they do not learn them when trained conventionally on computer vision tasks.

title: Iterative convergent computation may not be a useful inductive bias for residual neural networks
claim: Encouraging weight sharing (toward a recurrent ResNet) and convergence does not improve classification accuracy, including on occlusion tasks.
quote: However, neither recurrence regularization nor spectral normalization improve classification accuracy on standard visual recognition tasks (MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100) or on challenging recognition tasks with partial occlusions (Digitclutter).

title: Dynamic Recursive Neural Network
claim: Recursive blocks with adaptive loop gates reduce parameters and compute while outperforming the original model.
quote: Experiments show that the DRNN reduces the parameters and computational cost and while outperforms the original model in term of the accuracy consistently on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1k.

title: Dynamic Recursive Neural Network
claim: Recursive networks are hard to train; per-loop batch normalization stabilizes gradients.
quote: Since the recursive networks are hard to train, we propose the Loopy Variable Batch Normalization (LVBN) to stabilize the volatile gradient.

title: Deep Equilibrium Object Detection and Segmentation
claim: The DEQ decoder converges faster, uses less memory and outperforms the explicit multi-layer AdaMixer decoder.
quote: DEQDet converges faster, consumes less memory, and achieves better results than the baseline counterpart (AdaMixer).

title: Deep Equilibrium Non-Autoregressive Sequence Learning
claim: Solving for the equilibrium of the NAR refinement dynamics yields more accurate predictions and helps several NAR backbones.
quote: Our main findings show that D EQ NAR can indeed converge to a more accurate prediction and is a general-purpose framework that consistently helps yield substantial improvement for several strong NAR backbones.

title: Weight-Tied Adaptive Recursive Vision–Language–Action Transformer for Efficient Multimodal Robotic Control
claim: Recursive refinement cuts action MSE by 82.4% versus a non-recursive baseline at 1.5x inference overhead.
quote: The recursive model achieves a mean squared error (MSE) of 0.020, representing an 82.4\% reduction compared to the baseline (MSE: 0.1137).

title: One Wide Feedforward is All You Need
claim: Sharing the encoder or decoder FFN across layers costs only 0.2-0.3 BLEU while cutting parameters by nearly 20%.
quote: Sharing either the encoder (SharedEnc) or the decoder FFN (SharedDec) results in just a 0.2 to 0.3 B LEU point decrease, while reducing the parameter count by nearly 20%.

title: One Wide Feedforward is All You Need
claim: At the same parameter count, one wide shared encoder FFN with no decoder FFN improves BLEU (35.6 to 36.5) and decoding speed over Transformer Big.
quote: We propose increasing the dimension of the shared FFN to match the number of parameters of the original (fully-parameterized) model, so as to avoid increasing the overhead of model storage.

title: One Wide Feedforward is All You Need
claim: Attention is not as redundant as the FFN: sharing attention causes significant accuracy drops.
quote: important and not as redundant, as sharing the attention leads to significant accuracy drops.

title: Learning Graph Algorithms With Recurrent Graph Neural Networks
claim: Recurrent GNNs extrapolate to graphs up to 1000x larger than training, beating IterGNN; a non-recurrent GIN fails beyond training sizes.
quote: Both the RecGIN-E and RecGRU-E can extrapolate to graphs that are up to 1000 times larger than the graphs encountered during training, with the GRU variant achieving the best results overall.

title: Learning Graph Algorithms With Recurrent Graph Neural Networks
claim: Input skip connections are necessary for extrapolation, confirming Deep Thinking's recall finding for GNNs.
quote: This confirms the findings of Schwarzschild et al., that access to the input features is a crucial part of gaining extrapolation abilities.

title: Learning Graph Algorithms With Recurrent Graph Neural Networks
claim: Without state regularization accuracy collapses after about 100 rounds; with L2 regularization predictions stay stable for many more rounds.
quote: Afterwards, the models trained with L2 regularization still stay stable while accuracy declines rapidly without regularization.

title: EdgeFormer: A Parameter-Efficient Transformer for On-Device Seq2seq Generation
claim: Moderate parameter reuse in the encoder gives significant gains at fixed parameters, but gains become marginal once each parameter is reused more than about 6 times.
quote: moderately reusing parameters (e.g., when x ≤ 4) helps better utilize the parameters, resulting in significant performance gain without increasing parameters.

title: EdgeFormer: A Parameter-Efficient Transformer for On-Device Seq2seq Generation
claim: EdgeFormer without layer adaptation clearly outperforms Universal Transformer at comparable size and FLOPs; LoRA and prefix layer adaptation add further gains.
quote: According to Table 2, the E DGE F ORMER without layer adaptation (LA) largely outperforms UTs.

title: Compact and Optimal Deep Learning with Recurrent Parameter Generators
claim: At the same number of free parameters, RPG networks beat vanilla ResNets, and the deeper ResNet34-RPG beats ResNet18-RPG, i.e., more compute per parameter helps.
quote: ResNet34-RPG achieves higher accuracy than ResNet18RPG, indicating increasing time complexity gives performance gain.

title: Compact and Optimal Deep Learning with Recurrent Parameter Generators
claim: Reusing the MDEQ multiscale block 2-4 times at the same DoF beats MDEQ's fixed-point solution with 15-25x less inference time.
quote: At the same number of model DoF, RPG achieves 3% - 6% performance gain with 15 - 25x less inference time.

title: Compact and Optimal Deep Learning with Recurrent Parameter Generators
claim: A ResNet18 implemented with DoF of one conv layer still reaches 67.2% ImageNet top-1.
quote: a ResNet18 can be implemented with DoF equivalent to one convolution layer in a ResNet18-vanilla (4.72× DoF reduction) and still achieves 67.2% ImageNet top-1 accuracy.

title: RAFT: Recurrent All-Pairs Field Transforms for Optical Flow
claim: Tying the update operator weights across iterations gives better accuracy than untied per-iteration weights, with far fewer parameters.
quote: Here, we test a version of our approach where each update operator learns a separate set of weights. Accuracy is better when weights are tied and the parameter count is significantly lower.

title: RAFT: Recurrent All-Pairs Field Transforms for Optical Flow
claim: Trained with 12 unrolled updates, the model can run many more at inference, keeps improving, and does not diverge even at 200.
quote: Our method quickly converges, surpassing PWC-Net after 3 updates and FlowNet2 after 6 updates, but continues to improve with more updates.

title: RAFT: Recurrent All-Pairs Field Transforms for Optical Flow
claim: A gated (GRU) update block converges better than a plain 3-layer conv update.
quote: We achieve better performance by using the GRU block, likely because the gated activation makes it easier for the sequence of flow estimates to converge.

title: Recurrent Segmentation for Variable Computational Budgets
claim: Running the RNN for more iterations than trained keeps improving predictions.
quote: Interestingly, if one runs the network for more steps than it was originally trained, the RNN predictions continue to improve (Figure 5, blue curves) as the canvas saturates.

title: Recurrent Segmentation for Variable Computational Budgets
claim: Loss placement shapes the anytime curve: supervising early iterations helps early predictions but hurts the best result and breaks monotonic improvement.
quote: applying the loss to iteration three or earlier improved the prediction quality at earlier iterations, but decreased the quality of the best segmentation

title: Recurrent Segmentation for Variable Computational Budgets
claim: With many iterations, the RNN performs comparably to state-of-the-art feed-forward segmenters, but worse on high-spatial-frequency classes.
quote: When run for many iterations, the RNN performs comparably to state-of-the-art networks [21, 69, 8, 72, 9], but performs notably worse on specific classes that have high spatial frequency features

title: Bridging the Gaps Between Residual Learning, Recurrent Neural Networks and Visual Cortex
claim: A weight-shared (recurrent) ResNet with orders of magnitude fewer parameters performs similarly to the corresponding untied ResNet.
quote: A direct implementation of such a RNN, although having orders of magnitude fewer parameters, leads to a performance similar to the corresponding ResNet.

title: Bridging the Gaps Between Residual Learning, Recurrent Neural Networks and Visual Cortex
claim: Sharing weights in the first stage always helps, while sharing in later stages sometimes slightly hurts.
quote: sharing weights over time in the first stage of ResNet always improves performance. However, sharing weights in the later stages does sometimes slightly lower performance.

title: Bridging the Gaps Between Residual Learning, Recurrent Neural Networks and Visual Cortex
claim: At fixed parameters, longer unrolling (readout time) consistently lowers error.
quote: We observe in (D) and (E) that error reduces as t increases, while #param. is kept the same.

title: Bridging the Gaps Between Residual Learning, Recurrent Neural Networks and Visual Cortex
claim: Batch-norm statistics must be time-specific in recurrent nets; sharing them across time hurts.
quote: we found that it generally hurts performance when the normalization statistics (i.e., average, standard deviation) in batch normalization are shared across time.

title: Value Iteration Networks
claim: Untying the weights of the K recurrent VI layers (same effective depth, more parameters) degrades performance, most at small training-data sizes.
quote: Our results, in Table 2 show that untying the weights degrades performance, with a stronger effect for smaller sizes of training data.

title: Value Iteration Networks
claim: VINs outperform reactive CNN/FCN policies on grid-worlds, with the gap growing with problem size.
quote: For all domain sizes, VIN networks significantly outperform standard reactive networks. Note that the performance gap increases dramatically with problem size.

title: Understanding Deep Architectures using a Recursive Convolutional Network
claim: At constant parameters (tied model), adding layers improves performance, because more nonlinearities allow more complex functions.
quote: At these depths, therefore, adding more layers alone tends to increase performance, even though no additional parameters are introduced.

title: Understanding Deep Architectures using a Recursive Convolutional Network
claim: At the same depth and width, untied models (more parameters) beat tied ones, with the gap closing for the largest models.
