claim: Duplicating a validation-selected layer range of a frozen ViT improves downstream classification over the standard pass, without gradient training.
quote: At the maximum label budget, class-specific selection reaches a macro F1 of 0.875, closing the gap to the fully supervised ConvNeXt benchmark (0.889) to 1.4 points without any gradient-based training.

title: Refine Thought: A Test-Time Inference Method for Embedding Model Reasoning
claim: Iterative re-encoding gives marginal gains on BRIGHT and saturates after 2-3 iterations.
quote: Across BRIGHT subtasks, RT improves the overall average from 22.9 to 23.1 (≈ +1%, Table 2), indicating that additional reasoning steps bring marginal benefits to complex retrieval.

title: Recurrent Self-Attention Dynamics: An Energy-Agnostic Perspective from Jacobians
claim: Normalization layers control the Lipschitzness of looped self-attention and keep the dynamics near criticality, which correlates with high accuracy.
quote: It reveals that the normalization layer plays an essential role in suppressing the Lipschitzness of SA and the Jacobian’s complex eigenvalues, which correspond to the oscillatory components of the dynamics.

title: Recurrent Self-Attention Dynamics: An Energy-Agnostic Perspective from Jacobians
claim: Energy-based regularization underperforms while Jacobian spectral regularization improves accuracy.
quote: Energy-based regularization (“E-single” and “E-multi”) underperforms the original methods, while Jacobian spectral regularization (“Spec”) outperforms.

title: Quantifying the Necessity of Chain of Thought through Opaque Serial Depth
claim: The authors state that adding recurrence should allow long serial cognition in activations, weakening the argument that thinking out loud is necessary, and suggest one may want to avoid recurrent architectures for monitorability.
quote: For example, adding recurrence should enable long serial cognition within the activations, and so should reduce our expectation that thinking out loud is necessary.

title: Quantifying the Necessity of Chain of Thought through Opaque Serial Depth
claim: Under the framework, continuous latent chain of thought composes the full network T_cot times, so its opaque serial depth scales linearly with the number of latent steps.
quote: Assuming that we are using a Transformer architecture, each invocation of the 𝑓𝜃 has depth 𝑂 ( 𝐿 (log 𝑇 + log 𝐷)). Thus, the overall depth is 𝑂 ( 𝐿𝑇𝑐𝑜𝑡 (log 𝑇 + log 𝐷)).

title: Quantifying the Necessity of Chain of Thought through Opaque Serial Depth
claim: For a standard autoregressive Transformer every token is interpretable, so opaque depth is limited to one forward pass: O(L(log T + log D)).
quote: Thus, every layer has depth 𝑂 (log 𝑇 + log 𝐷). Since the overall forward pass is a composition of 𝐿 layers, the overall opaque serial depth is 𝑂 ( 𝐿 (log 𝑇 + log 𝐷)).

title: Quantifying the Necessity of Chain of Thought through Opaque Serial Depth
claim: An MoE Transformer with 11B active parameters has a calculated depth well below dense Gemma 3 12B, suggesting MoE lowers serial depth.
quote: The JAX calculator produces a depth of 4,096 for this model, which is significantly lower than the JAX-calculated depth of 11,268 for Gemma 3 12B, and even the by-hand calculation of 8,754 (Table 2)

title: A Pragmatic Way to Measure Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
claim: Monitorability can be lost through architectural change, explicitly including latent reasoning, so it must be measured to be preserved.
quote: Shifts in training practices, such as scaled-up reinforcement learning, or the adoption of architectures that rely on latent reasoning, threaten to degrade or eliminate this visibility.

title: A Pragmatic Way to Measure Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
claim: Current frontier reasoning models have high default legibility and coverage on difficult tasks.
quote: All models achieve very high scores, indicating that their necessary reasoning is highly monitorable by default.

title: A Pragmatic Way to Measure Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
claim: The metric measures default monitorability and does not replace adversarial stress-testing; it should not be used as a training objective.
quote: To preserve the integrity of these measures, we do not recommend using them as a training objective, as doing so risks Goodhart's law.

title: Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
claim: Reasoning models' CoTs often fail to verbalize hints they use, including misalignment-related hints.
quote: The overall faithfulness scores for both reasoning models remain low (25% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 39% for DeepSeek R1) (Figure 1).

title: Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
claim: Outcome-based RL improves faithfulness early but plateaus at moderate levels.
quote: Outcome-based RL initially increases CoT faithfulness substantially but plateaus at an average of 28% on MMLU and 20% on GPQA.

title: Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
claim: Behaviors that can be done within a single forward pass (e.g. intention faking) are unlikely to be verbalized, so CoT monitoring cannot rule them out.
quote: Moreover, intention faking does not seem like a reasoning-intensive task and can likely be done within single forward passes, making it unlikely to be faithfully verbalized in the CoT based on our experimental results.

title: Ulterior Motives: Detecting Misaligned Reasoning in Continuous Thought Models
claim: A continuous thought model can carry an armed misaligned latent state while producing moral outputs, and harmful output appears only when the release trigger is added.
quote: We observe that baseline, armed ([T]), and control ([O]) all produce moral outputs >91% of the time (94.2%, 91.7%, and 93.8%, respectively), confirming that [T] alone does not leak misaligned reasoning into outputs and [O] alone has no effect.

title: Ulterior Motives: Detecting Misaligned Reasoning in Continuous Thought Models
claim: Linear probes detect armed-but-benign latent states, most accurately at the earliest latent token, degrading toward chance at later tokens.
quote: Transfer accuracy peaks at z1 (89.4%) and degrades monotonically to near-chance at z6 (58.3%), confirming that probes detect armed latent states, not outputs.

title: Ulterior Motives: Detecting Misaligned Reasoning in Continuous Thought Models
claim: Results are limited to Coconut-style continuous thoughts; depth-recurrent Huginn and CODI are not evaluated.
quote: We evaluate only Coconut-style continuous thought models—other architectures like CODI and Huginn may exhibit different latent dynamics.

title: A Formal Framework for Understanding Length Generalization in Transformers
claim: Copying arbitrary strings and n-digit addition are not expressible by Limit Transformers, so any idealized solution sequence must grow depth, heads, norms, MLP size or precision with input length.
quote: As a consequence, any run of the Inference Procedure on these functions will output solutions T1 , T2 , T3 , . . . for which the depth, number of heads, parameter norms or ranks, MLP dimensions, or precision p, must increase with the input length n

title: A Formal Framework for Understanding Length Generalization in Transformers
claim: C-RASP expressiveness predicts empirical length generalization on regular languages: success exactly where a C-RASP[periodic, local] program was found.
quote: We found C-RASP[periodic,local] programs for 13 of the languages and proved nonexistence for the others (Appendix E.1.2). Length generalization succeeded in those cases where we had found a C-RASP[periodic,local] program (see Figure 1 right).

title: A Formal Framework for Understanding Length Generalization in Transformers
claim: The length-generalizable class (C-RASP[periodic, local]) is a proper subclass of TC0, suggesting a separation between TC0 and what fixed-depth APE Transformers length-generalize on.
quote: All problems considered in Section 5 are in TC0 , but empirical length generalization behavior largely tracks C-RASP[periodic,local] expressiveness, which defines a proper subclass of TC0 (Appendix C.3.1).

title: Lower Bounds for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Hard-Attention Transformers
claim: Any UHAT chain of thought for PARITY needs length linear in the input.
quote: In this model, we rigorously prove that the CoT for PARITY described above is optimal up to constant factors (Theorem 4.2).

title: Lower Bounds for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Hard-Attention Transformers
claim: Across PARITY, multiplication, median and reachability, CoT length must scale at least linearly, and the bounds are tight up to logarithmic factors.
quote: Across tasks, we show that CoT lengths need to scale at least linearly in the size of the original problem. We further show that our bounds are optimal up to logarithmic factors.

title: Lower Bounds for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Hard-Attention Transformers
claim: Filler-token (dot-by-dot) CoTs face an even stronger barrier: for PARITY their length cannot be polynomially bounded; the authors suggest logarithmic depth growth as a way around these limits.
quote: Logarithmic growth of the depth may be one way to overcome these (Merrill & Sabharwal, 2024b); within fixed-depth architectures, certain SSM architectures overcome at least the difficulty of PARITY (Grazzi et al., 2024).

title: Perfect diffusion is $\mathsf{TC}^0$ -- Bad diffusion is Turing-complete
claim: Perfect score-matching diffusion is limited to TC0 because its convergence is fast and does not scale with input length.
quote: In one direction, a network that exactly computes the score function of some initial distribution can only perform language modeling within the TC0 complexity class, reflecting limitations tied to rapid convergence.

title: Perfect diffusion is $\mathsf{TC}^0$ -- Bad diffusion is Turing-complete
claim: Without any score-matching requirement, diffusion dynamics can simulate any Turing machine via a non-convergent force field.
quote: By constructing a “bad” diffusion model with a specifically designed, non-convergent score function, we showed that such systems can achieve Turing-completeness, capable of simulating arbitrary sequential computation via a pinball machine analogy.

title: Perfect diffusion is $\mathsf{TC}^0$ -- Bad diffusion is Turing-complete
claim: Predicted empirical signature: more denoising steps beyond a threshold help little on TC0 tasks but keep helping on tasks outside TC0; the author proposes architectures that switch between sequential and parallel modes.
quote: Adding more denoising steps beyond a certain threshold should yield minimal improvements for TC0 tasks but continued improvements for tasks outside this complexity class.

title: Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems
claim: Without CoT, the serial computation of a Transformer is bounded by its depth; with T intermediate steps it grows to T, which can scale with input length while depth stays fixed.
quote: Intuitively, without CoT, the number of serial computations conducted by the transformer is bounded by the depth (which is considered as a fixed constant for this work), whereas with T intermediate steps, the number of serial computations possible is boosted to T .

title: Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems
claim: Constant-depth constant-precision Transformers without CoT are in AC0, but T CoT steps suffice to compute any size-T circuit.
quote: However, with T steps of CoT, constant-depth transformers using constant-bit precision and O(log n) embedding size can solve any problem solvable by boolean circuits of size T .

title: Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems
claim: Logarithmically many CoT steps add no power beyond AC0.
quote: Interestingly, we also show that logarithmically many CoT steps do not allow the transformer to compute functions beyond AC0 . (Theorem 3.1)

title: Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems
claim: Empirically, CoT drastically improves low-depth Transformers on inherently serial tasks; without CoT, S5 composition accuracy stays near chance.
quote: Note for the most time the accuracy without CoT is ∼ 20%, which is no better than randomly guessing a number between 1 and 5.

title: Continuous Chain of Thought Enables Parallel Exploration and Reasoning
claim: Continuous tokens let the model keep multiple reasoning traces in superposition and defer commitment, outperforming COCONUT, discrete CoT and no-CoT on search tasks; discrete CoT needs multiple samples to match single-shot CoT2.
quote: (a): Discrete CoT model requires multiple samplings (Pass@k) to match the single-shot performance of CoT2 model on MNNS (10-run avgs). (b): CoT2 model outperforms COCONUT, discrete CoT, and no-CoT in tasks involving search, like MNNS and ProsQA (5-run avgs).

title: Continuous Chain of Thought Enables Parallel Exploration and Reasoning
claim: Parallelism is capped by embedding capacity: superposing more traces helps only when the embedding dimension is large enough.
quote: This indicates a capacity–parallelism tradeoff in which larger B helps only when d is sufficiently large to represent the superposed traces.

title: Continuous Chain of Thought Enables Parallel Exploration and Reasoning
claim: The authors position CoT2 alongside looped Transformers as reasoning with continuous representations.
quote: Another line of work has found looped transformers to be effective on reasoning problems [Giannou et al., 2023, Geiping et al., 2025], notably being able to mimic CoT [Saunshi et al., 2025] with a sufficient number of iterations.

title: Quantization Robustness of Monotone Operator Equilibrium Networks
claim: Convergence of the quantized solver is guaranteed whenever the spectral-norm weight perturbation is smaller than the monotonicity margin, and the equilibrium shift is bounded.
quote: We provide an explicit quantizationpreservation certificate: a single computable check on the weight perturbation determines whether the quantized network retains existence, uniqueness, linear convergence, and a bounded displacement of its equilibrium.

title: Quantization Robustness of Monotone Operator Equilibrium Networks
claim: Empirically the divergence threshold matches the predicted ratio of perturbation to margin: 3- and 4-bit PTQ diverge, 5-bit and above converge.
quote: The non-convergence/convergence transition aligns with ∥∆W ∥2 /m = 1: 3-bit (ratio 5.36) and 4-bit (2.66) diverge, 5-bit and above converge.

title: Quantization Robustness of Monotone Operator Equilibrium Networks
claim: Quantization-aware training, made well defined by the backward-pass guarantee, recovers convergence at 4 bits where PTQ fails.
quote: Quantization-aware training recovers convergence at 4 bits where post-training quantization fails, enabled by the backward-pass guarantee of Theorem 5.

title: Fractal basins trap latent reasoning
claim: On hard instances, convergence time of recurrent reasoners is a fractal function of the initial latent state, so tiny initialization changes can change loops-to-converge by orders of magnitude.
quote: Across diverse reasoning models, we observe complex basins of attraction when we label initial conditions by their convergence time, and we find that these basins become self-similar fractals on harder tasks, like Sudoku puzzles (Fig. 1B).

title: Fractal basins trap latent reasoning
claim: Basin entropy strongly correlates with the mean number of loops needed to converge, a proxy for task difficulty.
quote: We find that the basin entropy strongly correlates with the number of iterations, a measure of overall task difficulty. These findings persist across alternative architectures (Appendix C) and basin complexity metrics (Appendix D).

title: Fractal basins trap latent reasoning
claim: Slow-converging trajectories are trapped near saddle points that decode to nearly-correct solutions.
quote: Decoding these meandering trajectories into problem states reveals that reasoning becomes trapped near answers that are nearly, but not quite, correct. In mazes, saddle regions correspond to dead ends; in Sudoku puzzles, they represent grids with repeated digits (Fig. 3D).

title: Fractal basins trap latent reasoning
claim: Fractal basins appear at a training bifurcation when the looped model acquires multi-step reasoning; incorrect fixed points become saddles.
quote: We thus find that the bifurcation to solvability during training occurs when the model gains multi-step reasoning capability. This, in turn, allows the model to escape from incorrect solutions in the core, but it leads to transient chaos and fractal basins.

title: Neural Cellular Automata for ARC-AGI
claim: Per-task NCAs with no pretraining solve a modest fraction of feasible ARC tasks perfectly.
quote: Thus, there were 172 feasible tasks. Of these, the NCA approach solved 23 perfectly, resulting in a success rate of 13.37%.

title: Neural Cellular Automata for ARC-AGI
claim: Supervising every step rather than only the final step was needed for stability and generalization, because errors compound across iterations.
quote: Small errors tend to compound over time; constant supervision mitigates this problem.

title: Neural Cellular Automata for ARC-AGI
claim: Learned local iterative rules can generalize in size: a spiral rule trained on small grids runs coherently on 100x100 grids by using more steps.
quote: The system learned a compact, iterative rule that is precise enough to have an effective degree of size invariance, capable of scaling up to a 100×100 grid (Figure 3).

title: State Representation and Termination for Recursive Reasoning Systems
claim: A small order-gap indicates that further iteration is unlikely to help; the main theorem says when this criterion is informative, as a local (not global) result.
quote: Our main result gives a necessary and sufficient condition for the linearised order-gap to be non-degenerate near the fixed point, showing when the criterion is informative rather than algebraically vacuous. This is a local condition, not a global convergence guarantee.

title: State Representation and Termination for Recursive Reasoning Systems
claim: Existing recursive systems including TRM leave state and termination implicit and do not derive termination from their operator structure.
quote: The RLM's aggregate state is an unstructured REPL buffer; the TRM's is a latent vector. Neither derives its termination criterion from the operator structure.

title: DACT-BERT: Differentiable Adaptive Computation Time for an Efficient BERT Inference
claim: At limited compute, DACT-BERT outperforms early-exit baselines on almost every GLUE task.
quote: On the other hand, when using limited amounts of computation our model outperforms the alternatives in almost every task, especially in tasks for with more training data available.

title: DACT-BERT: Differentiable Adaptive Computation Time for an Efficient BERT Inference
claim: Learned halting gives stable compute savings for a fixed ponder penalty, while entropy-threshold early exit is hyperparameter-sensitive.
quote: As the same values of ponder penalties give rise to similar efficiency outputs. By contrast, DeeBERT proves to be highly sensitive to the chosen value for the entropy hyperparameter.

title: DACT-BERT: Differentiable Adaptive Computation Time for an Efficient BERT Inference
claim: Halting is triggered when further blocks cannot change the predicted class, not by a confidence threshold.
quote: That is, the model stops executing additional blocks once it finds that doing so will not change the class with maximum probability in the output because the difference between the top class and the rest is insurmountable.

title: Hyper-Connections
claim: Dynamic hyper-connections make an MoE LM converge 1.8x faster and improve ARC-Challenge by 6 points at 500B tokens.
quote: The model utilizing DHC converges 1.8 times faster and shows an improvement of 6 points on ARC-Challenge compared to the baseline trained with 500 B tokens.

title: Hyper-Connections
claim: Pre-Norm baselines show representation collapse (high adjacent-layer similarity); HC lowers that similarity, suggesting each layer contributes more.
quote: According to our visualization analysis, as shown in Fig.3, the baseline model tends toward representation collapse, characterized by high similarity between features of adjacent layers.

title: Hyper-Connections
claim: Expansion rate matters: a single stream (n = 1) is worse than baseline; n > 1 helps, saturating at n = 4.
quote: We observe that with an expansion rate of n = 1, the performance of DHC is inferior to the baseline. However, for n > 1, DHC significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving superior results at n = 4, with the increase to n = 8 providing minimal additional benefits.

title: The State-Prediction Separation Hypothesis
claim: SPS reaches standard-Transformer validation loss with far fewer training tokens; doubling the standard model's token budget does not close the gap.
quote: At 1.6B parameters, State-Prediction Separation matches the validation loss of a standard Transformer trained on 47B tokens while using 2.6× fewer tokens (pre-decay).

title: The State-Prediction Separation Hypothesis
claim: Gains carry to held-out corpora and zero-shot tasks at the same persistent KV footprint and near-equal throughput.
quote: SPS's persistent KV cache is the same size as S TANDARD's (peak memory ratio 1.01), and end-to-end throughput is within 6–10% of S TANDARD at all scales.

title: The State-Prediction Separation Hypothesis
claim: Committing persistent state at the later (prediction) step, which gives the same extra compute without separation, is consistently worse than SPS.
quote: D ELAYED S TATE does improve over S TANDARD, confirming that the extra computation step carries some benefit, but at every scale SPS remains consistently better, by 0.019–0.021 in validation NLL and by 0.06–0.07 in corpus NLL (Table 2).

title: The State-Prediction Separation Hypothesis
claim: Keeping every prediction-step entry persistent (double memory) is worse than SPS with half the persistent cache, so the gain is not capacity-based.
quote: SPS is consistently better in validation NLL across XS–XL, even though it has half the persistent KV cache. This shows that the gain is not capacity-based.

title: The Neural Data Router: Adaptive Control Flow in Transformers Improves Systematic Generalization
claim: NDR achieves perfect length generalization on compositional table lookup, which no previous neural network had reported.
quote: Our novel Neural Data Router (NDR) achieves 100% length generalization accuracy on the classic compositional table lookup task, as well as near-perfect accuracy on the simple arithmetic task and a new variant of ListOps testing for generalization across computational depths.

title: The Neural Data Router: Adaptive Control Flow in Transformers Improves Systematic Generalization
claim: On ListOps, baselines reach near-perfect IID accuracy but fail on deeper test problems, while NDR generalizes.
quote: Like on the other tasks, the baseline LSTM and Transformers do not generalize well on the test set consisting of deeper problems, while they achieve a near-perfect accuracy on IID data. In contrast, our model achieves near-perfect generalization.

title: The Neural Data Router: Adaptive Control Flow in Transformers Improves Systematic Generalization
claim: Generalization requires shared-layer depth at least as large as the computation depth.
quote: We clearly observe that, while the shallow models can also solve the IID split, only the deep models generalize to the longer problems (here the 12-layer model generalizes almost perfectly, but the 10-layer one does not).

title: The Neural Data Router: Adaptive Control Flow in Transformers Improves Systematic Generalization
claim: Because parameters are shared, more steps can be run at test time than in training without a penalty.
quote: We did this for the ListOps experiment (Sec. 3.3): the model was trained with 20 layers and tested with 24. Our preliminary experiments confirmed that this practice has no performance penalty, while it speeds up training.

title: A rigor-matched audit of periodic-step layer skipping for efficient llm inference: conflayers versus swift, with a supplemental analysis of trained routing alternatives
claim: Among periodic-step methods, SWIFT has the best accuracy in three of four task/scale cells and ConfLayers is dominated everywhere, worst on GSM8K at 1.5B.
quote: SWIFT is the strongest method on accuracy in three of four cells; ConfLayers is dominated everywhere, with particularly large deficits on GSM8K at 1.5B.

title: A rigor-matched audit of periodic-step layer skipping for efficient llm inference: conflayers versus swift, with a supplemental analysis of trained routing alternatives
claim: Folding online-search time into wall-clock latency inverts the speed ranking: SWIFT's pure inference is 5-21% faster than ConfLayers's in all cells although its total wall-clock is slower in three of four.
quote: once decomposed, SWIFT's pure inference cost is faster than ConfLayers's in all four cells (5-21%), reversing the naive ranking in three of them.

title: A rigor-matched audit of periodic-step layer skipping for efficient llm inference: conflayers versus swift, with a supplemental analysis of trained routing alternatives
claim: Trained routers give real but modest measured speedups that are smaller than the savings implied by the number of skipped layers, attributed to per-layer router overhead.
quote: both methods show modest but real speedups (1.08–1.33×) over a genuine full-model baseline, smaller than layer-count-implied theoretical savings would suggest; we attribute this to LayerRoute's router computation

title: A rigor-matched audit of periodic-step layer skipping for efficient llm inference: conflayers versus swift, with a supplemental analysis of trained routing alternatives
claim: Per-sequence trained gating collapses on multi-step reasoning at 1.5B.
quote: LayerRoute's accuracy on GSM8K at 1.5B is essentially zero (0.003 mean, 1 of 300 samples correct)

title: A rigor-matched audit of periodic-step layer skipping for efficient llm inference: conflayers versus swift, with a supplemental analysis of trained routing alternatives
claim: All latency numbers are batch-size-1 single-GPU measurements with explicit synchronization and no warm-up.
quote: All latency measurements use batch size 1 on a single GPU, with explicit device synchronization before and after each timed call

title: Does per-frame early exit pay? A compute-matched study of dynamic depth for on-device speech enhancement
claim: Once fixed-depth models are compared fairly, per-frame routing adds little: the extracted static models form a competitive frontier, also under measured latency.
quote: once the fixeddepth models are compared fairly, routing brings little advantage: indeed, the extracted static models form a competitive quality–compute frontier, which holds when considering measured latency instead of theoretical MACs.

title: Does per-frame early exit pay? A compute-matched study of dynamic depth for on-device speech enhancement
claim: Within one fixed ladder, early exit does cut measured on-device latency with little quality loss.
quote: At H=256, routing reduces latency from 2.472 to 1.668,ms/frame while retaining 2.773 versus 2.781 PESQ.

title: Does per-frame early exit pay? A compute-matched study of dynamic depth for on-device speech enhancement
claim: Analytic MACs do not predict accelerator latency: time per MMAC varies 1.7x across topologies and MAC count can invert the latency ordering.
quote: MAC count can even give the wrong ordering: (H=96, R=1) uses 21 % more MACs than (H=32, R=2) but runs 15 % faster.

title: Does per-frame early exit pay? A compute-matched study of dynamic depth for on-device speech enhancement
claim: Without the repair, deeper exits are worse than shallower ones on nearly half of the frames (overthinking), and this is where routing's apparent benefit comes from.
quote: The apparent routing opportunity largely come from frames where deeper exits degrade the result, and the monotonicity repair removes much of that signal.

title: Does per-frame early exit pay? A compute-matched study of dynamic depth for on-device speech enhancement
claim: Common offline evaluation of routed models (gated sum) is optimistic because it updates the state of skipped stacks; deployed skipping keeps stale state.
quote: This is far more realistic than common offline evaluation protocols, which compute the routed output as a gated sum, thereby effectively updating each exit even when unused.

title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
claim: Up to about half of the layers can be removed with minimal QA degradation for some open-weight models.
quote: we find minimal degradation of performance until after a large fraction (up to half) of the layers are removed for some common open-weight models.

title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
claim: The pruning fraction at which QA accuracy collapses to random depends strongly on the model family.
quote: a sharp transition to random accuracy at a pruning fraction around 45%-55% for models in the Llama-2 family, 35% for Mistral 7B, 25% for Phi-2, and 20% for models from the Qwen family.

title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
claim: Reasoning tasks are not robust: GSM8K and HellaSwag degrade with any amount of pruning, tracking the loss increase.
quote: both GSM8K and HellaSwag, our two reasoning tasks, exhibit immediate degradation in performance with any amount of pruning, correlating with a similar decrease in the perplexity evals

title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
claim: Next-token loss on C4 degrades smoothly in proportion to the pruned fraction even where QA is flat.
quote: if we look at the loss on next-token predictions for an IID dataset (C4 validation set), we find that the model is smoothly damaged in proportion to the fraction of the number of layers pruned.

title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
claim: Deeper layers are more similar to their neighbors than shallow layers, except the final layer, so dropping the deepest block (excluding the last layer) nearly matches the similarity-informed choice after healing.
quote: after healing the damage with a small amount of QLoRA finetuning, we can achieve performance that nearly matches the more involved similarity-informed layer pruning strategy.

title: Megrez2 Technical Report
claim: Sharing each expert's parameters across n consecutive layers lowers total parameters by roughly n while activated parameters are unchanged.
quote: cross-layer expert sharing reduces the number of unique parameters by roughly a factor of n while keeping the activated parameters unchanged.

title: Megrez2 Technical Report
claim: Megrez2-Preview uses groups of three layers sharing a 64-expert pool after one dense first layer.
quote: The model consists of 31 layers in total, with the first layer being a dense layer. Every three layers form a group that shares the expert parameters of the MoE module, which includes 64 experts per group.

title: Megrez2 Technical Report
claim: Megrez2-Preview is reported competitive with or better than larger public models; the comparison is against public checkpoints trained on different data.
quote: With only 3B activated and 7.5B stored parameters, Megrez2-Preview demonstrates competitive or superior performance compared to larger models on a wide range of tasks

title: Megrez2 Technical Report
claim: Within a sharing group, an expert already selected does not have to be reloaded, which is the systems motivation for combining sharing with pre-gating.
quote: within a group whose layers share a common expert pool, an expert that has already been selected need not be re-loaded, allowing the cache size and replacement policy to be tuned to the available hardware.

title: MiniViT: Compressing Vision Transformers with Weight Multiplexing
claim: Naive cross-layer weight sharing in ViTs makes training unstable and can collapse it as more layers are shared.
quote: weight sharing across transformer layers makes the training become unstable, and even causes training collapse as the number of shared layers increases

title: MiniViT: Compressing Vision Transformers with Weight Multiplexing
claim: At equal depth and data, plain sharing halves parameters but costs about 2 points of top-1 accuracy.
quote: After applying the weight-sharing method, the numbers of parameters of both models are halved, whereas the accuracy also decreases by 2% (#1 vs. #2, #6 vs. #7).

title: MiniViT: Compressing Vision Transformers with Weight Multiplexing
claim: LayerNorm must not be shared across reused blocks because features at different depths have different statistics.
quote: the layer normalization [5] in different transformer blocks should not be identical during parameter sharing, because the features of different layers have various scales and statistics.

title: MiniViT: Compressing Vision Transformers with Weight Multiplexing
claim: With transformations plus distillation from a larger teacher, a model with half the layer parameters exceeds the original; this headline gain is confounded by distillation from an ImageNet-22k teacher.
quote: with the proposed weight multiplexing, the Mini-Swin-B model with 12-layer parameters obtains 0.8% higher accuracy than the 24-layer Swin-B.

title: MiniViT: Compressing Vision Transformers with Weight Multiplexing
claim: Extreme sharing (one layer of parameters) loses 2 points but cuts DeiT-B parameters 9.7x.
quote: MiniDeiT-B with 9M parameters achieves 79.8% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet, being 9.7 times smaller than DeiT-B (with 86 parameters and 81.8% accuracy).

title: Fixed Point Diffusion Models
claim: FPDM has 87% fewer parameters and 60% less training memory than DiT and better image quality when sampling compute or time is limited.
quote: Compared to the state-of-the-art DiT model, FPDM contains 87% fewer parameters, consumes 60% less memory during training, and improves image generation quality in situations where sampling computation or time is limited.

title: Fixed Point Diffusion Models
claim: The advantage disappears and reverses at larger sampling budgets.
quote: At 560 forward passes, our method outperforms DiT with DDPM but not DDIM, and for more than 560 it is outperformed by DiT.

title: Fixed Point Diffusion Models
claim: At matched per-timestep depth (26 iterations equal DiT's 28 layers) FPDM is slightly worse; its gains come from spreading the same compute over more timesteps.
quote: Although our model is slightly worse than DiT at 26 iterations, it significantly outperforms DiT when smoothed across more timesteps, demonstrating the effectiveness of timestep smoothing.

title: Fixed Point Diffusion Models
claim: The 1-step (Jacobian-free) gradient common in DEQs fails to optimize at ImageNet scale; multi-step and stochastic multi-step truncated unrolling work.
quote: We find that 1-step gradient, the most common method for training DEQ [5] models, struggles to optimize models on the large-scale ImageNet dataset, whereas a multi-step version of it performs well

title: Fixed Point Diffusion Models
claim: Allocating more fixed-point iterations to later denoising steps beats constant or decreasing allocation.
quote: the increasing heuristic outperforms the contant and decreasing ones; allocating resources more toward the later stages of the denoising process improves generation quality and detail.

title: Deep Equilibrium Optical Flow Estimation
claim: DEQ flow estimators train with 4-6x less memory than their unrolled recurrent counterparts and allow faster inference via reuse and inexact gradients.
quote: The use of these DEQ flow estimators allows us to compute the flow faster using, e.g., fixed-point reuse and inexact gradients, consumes 4 ∼ 6× less training memory than the recurrent counterpart

title: Deep Equilibrium Optical Flow Estimation
claim: Unrolled RAFT refinement does not converge: activations oscillate after about 15 iterations.
quote: while RAFT's iterative unrolling aims to mimic the iterative convergence, we find its activations usually oscillate at a relatively high level after about 15 update iterations.

title: Deep Equilibrium Optical Flow Estimation
